#3051. Apple Watch SE 3 vs Series 12: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up…

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”

With the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

What do you think of the current Apple Watch lineup? Are you shopping for one this holiday season? Let us know down in the comments.

#3050. Stock Market Today, Nov. 23: CoreWeave Surges 22% as Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

Today, Nov. 23, 2026, AI cloud names rallied as CoreWeave closed sharply higher on renewed sector optimism and heavy trading volume.

By Howard Smith – Nov 23, 2026 at 4:49PM EST

CoreWeave (CRWV +22.32%), a specialized cloud infrastructure provider for generative AI workloads, closed at $48.33, up 22.32%. Monday's advance followed renewed AI-sector optimism after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and investors are now watching AI demand and capital spending.Trading volume reached 93.2 million shares, coming in about 91% above its three-month average of 48.9 million shares. CoreWeave IPO'd in 2025 and has grown 21% since going public.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.73%) closed at 7,237, up 4.73%, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +6.51%) finished at 24,090, up 6.51%. In specialized cloud infrastructure and AI computing services, Nebius Group rose 20.28% to $97.80, and Iren climbed 23.86% to $14.64 as AI cloud names advanced together.

The Nvidia news clearly drove today's move, and for good reason. Nvidia not only owns almost 11% of CoreWeave, but it has also committed over $6 billion in business to CoreWeave. CoreWeave disclosed the order in late 2025, and it requires Nvidia to buy any cloud capacity CoreWeave doesn't sell to customers through April 2032.

CoreWeave is also dependent on the overall financial strength and capital spending of AI labs, hyperscalers, and other businesses. In its third-quarter report earlier this month, CoreWeave raised 2026 guidance, and now expects revenue growth to reach up to 160%, citing AI infrastructure demand strength. Nvidia is the backbone of that strength in many ways, and investors in CoreWeave will also need to believe that Nvidia remains on track despite the Jensen Huang scandal.

#3049. Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

Introducing Claude Ship (beta): Claude can review your pull requests, work on fixes, and approve the ones your team's policy allows.The goal is to help you ship code as fast as you can write it. pic.twitter.com/b9OBAhEBmr

Before Ted Lasso returned this year, Jason Sudeikis shared that he had a new three-season arc in mind. Apple’s Eddy Cue also suggested the company would be happy to continue making more seasons for years to come.

But until today’s announcement, the lack of official news still put Lasso fans’ hopes on pause.

Whether it returns in 2027 or, perhaps more likely 2028, Ted Lasso isn’t going away again anytime soon.

#3046. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

Scotto ranks No. 175 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.2%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.

On Nov. 23, 2026, investors rotated back into AI-chip names, with sector sentiment lifting shares across the group.

By Will Healy – Nov 23, 2026 at 4:50PM EST

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +6.85%), an AI and CPU chips provider, closed at $453.46, up 6.85%. Shares rose after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and investors are watching AI-chip sentiment and conference commentary.Trading volume reached 53.0M shares, coming in about 93% above its three-month average of 27.5M shares.

When it comes to TVs, I'll be the first to admit I care more about aesthetics than performance. If I could hide mine entirely, I would. That's why Hisense's Canvas TV was so appealing when it first hit the market. A big, blank screen had become an unwanted focal point in my otherwise thoughtfully decorated living room, and I wanted a better-looking alternative without paying a premium for Samsung's Frame TV.

I’ve incorporated the Canvas TV into gallery walls in multiple apartments and now my own home with ease, surrounding it with matted photographs, framed artwork, and other decorative objects. And just in time for Black Friday, Amazon has the Hisense 55-inch Hi-QLED CanvasTV on sale for $697. That's a massive 53% off with multiple screen sizes on sale.

The 2026 update of the Canvas TV pairs a crisp 4K picture with rich, vibrant Hi-QLED color and Dolby Vision support for enhanced contrast and detail. The 144Hz refresh rate helps reduce blur, whether you’re watching sports or playing video games. Plus, the new AI ambient light sensor automatically adjusts the screen’s brightness and color temperature to suit the lighting in your room, so you don’t have to waste time tweaking with the settings. It also runs on Google TV, giving you access your favorite apps without the need for an additional streaming device.

When we first reviewed the Canvas TV in 2024, we praised it as a value-friendly Samsung Frame TV dupe. It wasn’t without a few shortcomings, though. Our review found that the display could be quite dim, and that darker scenes often lacked detail and a cinematic feel. The original model was also limited to just two size options.

Hisense has made some worthwhile refinements over the years. While we haven’t officially reviewed the 2026 model, the improved Hi-Matte display is designed to do an even better job at minimizing glare and mimicking the appearance of art, while increased brightness should provide a more enjoyable viewing experience. The newer lineup also offers more sizes, ranging from 50 to 85 inches, along with additional frame finishes.

The latest version retains the very details that first made me a fan, however. I’m particularly fond of the included magnetic teak frame (no need to shell out for a separate decorative bezel!) and the ultra-slim wall mount that allows it to sit almost flush against the wall above my fireplace. That said, I was equally happy letting it rest directly on my console in a former rental, where my landlord wouldn't allow TV mounts.

Perhaps my favorite upgrade? The art library has expanded from a few hundred to over 1,000 complimentary choices.

So if you, like me, would rather have art than a giant blank screen as your living room centerpiece, this is the Black Friday TV deal worth considering.

#3039. iOS 27.2 upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new

Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27, but the recent release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And in iOS 27.2, Apple introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

What do you think of the latest Apple Photos changes in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3037. Apple Pay just got even better with four new features and more

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a new “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

#3036. Crypto Market Today, Nov. 23: Bitcoin Sits Out Wall Street's Historic Rally as $1.8 Billion ETF Exodus Weighs on Prices

Wall Street's dramatic recovery failed to deliver a boost to cryptocurrencies, exposing persistent weakness in investor demand despite improving sentiment across traditional financial markets.

By RJ Fulton – Nov 23, 2026 at 4:55PM EST

Cryptocurrency markets struggled to gain momentum on Monday, November 23, even as Wall Street staged a historic recovery following last week's sharp sell-off. Despite the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +6.51%) surging 6.51% and the S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.73%) gaining 4.74%, major digital assets remained largely unchanged, highlighting persistent weakness in investor demand.

As of early evening, Bitcoin (BTC -2.13%) was up just 0.08% to $61,213.38, while Ethereum (ETH -1.38%) slipped 0.09% to $1,719.49. Solana (SOL -1.47%) bucked the broader trend, gaining 2.84% to $72.57.

Cryptocurrency markets continue to face substantial selling pressure following last week's sharp decline, which pushed Bitcoin to a two-year low near $55,000 and sent other major digital assets to fresh bear market lows. Although prices have recovered modestly, the magnitude of the recent downturn has undermined investor confidence, with buying demand remaining insufficient to support a broader recovery.

Institutional capital flows have added to these challenges. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $1.8 billion in net outflows last week, reflecting continued withdrawals from cryptocurrency investment products. These outflows have removed an important source of buying demand at a time when broader market sentiment remains fragile.

U.S.-listed cryptocurrency ETFs rebounded on Monday following last week's steep losses. The iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT +4.85%) gained 4.85%, while the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC +5.08%) climbed 5.11%. Meanwhile, the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA +8.01%) surged 8.01%, outperforming its Bitcoin counterparts.

The cryptocurrency market's inability to participate in Monday's historic equity rally raises concerns about the strength of underlying investor demand. Despite recovering modestly from recent lows, major cryptocurrencies continue to struggle with persistent selling pressure and the absence of sustained ETF inflows. Without a meaningful return of capital, any recovery will likely face considerable resistance from investors looking to exit positions established at higher prices.

For Bitcoin, the $70,000 to $75,000 range could prove particularly challenging. The sharp decline through these levels has left investors holding substantial unrealized losses, potentially creating additional selling pressure as prices recover. Ethereum and Solana face similar challenges following their recent declines, with both requiring stronger buying demand to reclaim lost ground.

With major stock indexes recovering sharply but financial conditions still restrictive, renewed weakness in equities could quickly spill over into digital assets. Until institutional flows stabilize and cryptocurrencies demonstrate sustained buying pressure, the risk of another leg lower remains elevated.

Over the last two years, AI greed has been largely to blame for rising prices across the tech world, from video game consoles to phones and laptops. It may have just claimed another victim, like Jason slowly tromping through Camp Crystal Lake.

A new report from the Korean publication ETNews claims that Samsung will be shifting from an annual release of its Galaxy Watch lineup to a biennial cycle. By skipping 2027, the Galaxy Watch 10 would be the first one to not be released annually since Samsung debuted its first Galaxy smartwatch in 2018.

Now, as ETNews points out, "chipflation" is only partially to blame for this potential shift. However, it's certainly a major portion of it.

Samsung's Mobile eXperience (MX) division, responsible for the tech giant's smartphones, wearables, and more, has posted for profit losses for two quarters. The whole division is going through some major restructuring. That starts with Won-Joon Choi who was just announced as the new head of MX, less than four days ago.

Choi was previously the division's COO and led the launches of the S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8 series.

Tom's Guide reached out to Samsung for confirmation but did not receive a response in time for publication. We will update this article if the company responds.

The decision to delay the next Galaxy Watch is part of an aggressive push to make Samsung's mobile division more profitable. Part of that is streamlining the company's product lineup.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The increased prices of RAM and other key components have severely cut into Samsung's costs. Much of it is driven by Samsung's own chip fabrication division, which has fed into the AI chip frenzy.

Already, the company is reportedly cutting smartphone shipments by 30% with a focus on high-end models. A focus on premium, high-end models isn't new; other companies like Lenovo have already pursued it this year.

But also, the Galaxy Watch 9, a perfectly solid smartwatch, didn't move the needle when it debuted this summer. Plus, it suffered from a price hike as well. We praised the health insights that Samsung hasn't paywalled, unlike rivals, but at the end of the day its a more expensive Galaxy Watch 8. We didn't even include it in our picks for best smartwatch, a rarity for Samsung's usually excellent wearable.

“As hardware innovation has reached a mature stage, the company appears to have concluded that releasing new products every year is no longer cost-effective," industry insiders told ETNews.

According to ETNews, the gap year could be filled in by new software updates and enhancements to existing health tracking features.

Also, Samsung may release its own Galaxy Fit model à la the recently released Google Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air. Samsung has had versions, but nothing new has really hit in the last three years. Though at the beginning of November, a new fitness track was leaked as potential rival to the Fitbit Edge.

Perhaps, RAMageddon aside, this should be the model. In recent years, excitement for new phones, watches, and other annual tech hasn't really hit because, like EA Sports' ongoing Madden franchise, these iterative updates typically don't really justify the cost of upgrading.

Besides, Samsung already does this with the "Classic" model and the newer Galaxy Watch Ultra high-end watch, both of which are on two year cycles.

A year or more of development time could finally bring about true innovation and change.

#3032. Prediction: This Will Be Sandisk’s Stock Price by the End of 2027

Massive revenue growth and strengthening headwinds in AI will likely define the memory giant's destiny over the next year.

By Will Healy – Nov 23, 2026 at 4:56PM EST

Sandisk (SNDK +10.69%) has been one of the more notable tech growth stories over the last two years. After Western Digital spun it back off in February of last year, the stock rose by as much as 6,400%.

Unfortunately, the stock began a dramatic downturn from that peak over the summer, and it’s now down by more than 70% from its high. That did not stop Sandisk management from initiating an 8-for-1 stock split that took place Friday. Nonetheless, that volatility calls the stock's state into question, particularly when you’re trying to predict where it will trade at the end of 2027.

When comparing the company's continued growth and the expectations surrounding its industry, I believe Sandisk stock could end 2027 in the $170-per-share range.

Sandisk operates in one of the most volatile parts of the tech industry: memory. It specializes in NAND, a non-volatile type of memory that is used for longer-term storage, as well as in solid-state drives.

Western Digital bought the company back in 2016, but since it spun it back off again as a separate company, Sandisk has prospered. The rapid surge in AI data center construction has led to a severe shortage of the types of memory it supplies, giving Sandisk unusually strong pricing power. The result has been soaring revenues, wide profit margins, and a much higher stock price.

Unfortunately for investors, memory-chip makers are among the most volatile players in the chip industry. Memory products are fairly commoditized — there’s not a lot of differentiation between the NAND made by Sandisk and that sold by its direct peers. For this reason, prices are tightly linked to the supply-and-demand dynamic. Eventually, supply will catch up to demand and Sandisk will lose much of its pricing power.

Additionally, despite rapid growth, headwinds in the AI industry are emerging as investors question whether it can maintain current levels of capital expenditures (capex) amid rising interest rates. If capital becomes more scarce, the pace of the AI build-out could slow.

All of those conditions make it difficult to tell whether Sandisk is a bargain or a value trap.

Right now, Sandisk trades at around 5 times earnings. However, memory stock investors know the both revenue and profits can reverse dramatically during an industry downturn. History suggests that investors should not perceive that valuation as a "bargain."

Despite those risks, Sandisk's immediate future appears too compelling to dismiss.

In its fiscal 2027, which will end in July 2027, analysts forecast it will bring in just under $50 billion in revenue. If that prediction proves accurate, it will amount to a 145% year-over-year increase. Analysts also expect net earnings of $28.44 per share. On a split-adjusted basis, it earned $8.86 per share in its fiscal 2026.

Looking forward into fiscal 2028, analysts forecast revenue growth will slow to 24%. That could generate negative sentiment, but the $36.13 in consensus earnings expected that year would leave the P/E ratio at 2.4 at the current share price of $79 per share. That appears unreasonably low.

Nonetheless, whatever the sentiment, $28.44 per share multiplied by 6 — a common earnings multiple for memory stocks — would leave Sandisk with an approximate price of $170 per share. That factor alone makes it difficult to believe that Sandisk will not rise again.

Considering the forces that will likely pull Sandisk in opposing directions, I believe the stock will end 2027 in the neighborhood of $170, and trading at a P/E of about 6.

Admittedly, with the stock seemingly in free fall now, this might be a controversial call. The pricing power that Sandisk commands for now could disappear if the AI bubble bursts.

However, for now, an AI bust is more fear than reality. Additionally, we know that Sandisk’s bottom line will be far higher by the end of 2027. Unless the industry completely falls apart, it is hard to imagine that Sandisk stock will not trade at a much higher price by the end of next year.

#3031. Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me

In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road.

Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two.

To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes

“With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email.

Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats.

ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.”

Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3029. Your Googlebook just got a Chrome update – 5 new features

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Chrome update includes more useful vertical tabs, easier screen sharing, and some handy keyboard shortcuts.

On Monday, Google rolled out an M157 update for the Chrome web browser on Googlebook OS, with a handful of new features and performance boosts to streamline your workflow and browsing experience.

While the first Googlebooks on the market have received mixed reviews, these features could help the laptops gain more useful features in Chrome that other browsers already offer.

Also: Googlebooks? The best laptop for Android users is something else

Here are the five new Chrome features on Googlebook OS to know about.

If you’ve ever had to share your screen on a video call, you know how irritating it can be to switch tabs without having to repeatedly start and stop sharing. This Chrome update adds a tab-sharing controls bar; when you share a browser tab in a video call, Chrome will display a persistent control bar at the top of the window so you can “Stop sharing” or “Share this tab instead” from any tab.

Also: 6 Chrome default settings I changed to instantly

When you hover over a collapsed vertical tab rail with your mouse or trackpad, it will expand, so you can read full tab titles, switch tabs, or manage groups. The rail will collapse again when you move the cursor away.

This auto-expand feature is enabled by default. If you want to turn it off or on, go to Settings > Appearance > Tab position > “Auto expand tabs on hover,” or right-click the vertical tab rail.

The Chrome update allows you to manually resize your vertical tab bar to view longer page titles when needed. The browser will remember your custom tab width, even after you open a new window or restart the browser. (You’ll just need to turn “Auto expand tabs on hover” off for it to work.)

The system’s “Save As” file picker is now enabled by default for menu save actions, such as “Save link as” and “Save image as,” so you can more easily rename files and select a destination folder. This includes Google Drive or external storage.

Also: Google Chrome running slow? 5 easy ways to speed it up fast

Outside of these new features, a few of Chrome M157’s performance fixes include the ability to press Ctrl+L to reveal and select web addresses; keeping your bookmarks bar visible in fullscreen mode and while screen sharing; better media controls while using Picture-in-Picture mode; and the ability to partially translate PDFs within your browser.

If you have Chrome set up to automatically download and install updates, you won’t have to lift a finger to take advantage of the new features and performance boosts.

But if you’ve disabled automatic updates, you can manually update by selecting the three-dot menu in the top-right corner of your Chrome window and navigating to Help > About Google Chrome > Relaunch.

Also: My week with new Googlebooks: The good, the bad, and the promising

If the Relaunch option is greyed out or nowhere to be found, you’re running on the latest version of Chrome. And if you were working on something before the update, don’t worry: Chrome will save your open tabs and reopen them automatically when you restart.

Google is retiring Gemini Gems. Here's what to do to access the same tools as Skills.

Google is replacing Gemini Gems with Skills starting Nov. 17, 2026, and it’s carrying over features that let you share Skills and add files from Google products.

Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini. Any Gems you have created will automatically convert, but you can transfer them manually if you want to start using them now.

While the Gemini Gems feature is technically going away, any Gems you’ve created aren’t.

If you access the Gems portion of Gemini (since the feature is on the way out, you now have to access this through Settings), you’ll see a message that says “Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.” (The cutoff date for accessing your Gems will be Dec. 16, 2026. Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will get cut off in March 2027, and Workspace education accounts will be cut off in June 2027.)

A Gemini Skill functions much the same as a Gem. You describe specific situations when Gemini should use the Skill automatically and tell Gemini what you want the Skill to do (it’s best to give specific examples of output). Google gives the example of a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook.

The biggest difference is that Gems were standalone chats, while Skills are custom instructions that work in any conversation.

You can create as many Skills as you want, but only 100 can be active at a time.

To get users familiar with Skills, Google is bringing over two features from Gems.

First, you can now share any Skill with other users. When you share a Skill, you can choose whether the other person has permission to edit or view only. To share a Skill, go to the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills. You can view or change permissions from that screen.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

When a Skill is added, Gemini can use it automatically, or you can @mention it in chat to trigger it. One small caveat, though: you can only share Skills through the Gemini web app at the moment, not the mobile app.

Additionally, when you’re creating a Gemini Skill, you can choose to include files of up to 100MB from other Google products like Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with files from your local device. Gemini will reference these files every time the Skill runs and update in real time, Google says. These features existed with Gems; Google is just moving them to Skills to make the new feature more comparable.

‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ and more are streaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This week’s slate of new movies across the best streaming services is set, and with 14 new arrivals, you've got plenty of options to consider. That’s why I’ve combed through the full list and picked out some highlights on platforms including Netflix, HBO Max, Hulu and Apple TV.

The biggest newcomer this week is actually on premium streaming. The movie that everybody has been talking about will be available to watch at home; I, of course, refer to “You Can See Everything.” Alternatively, Netflix has a new WWII movie, HBO Max has a fantastical adventure great for young’uns, and Hulu has an entertaining buddy-style action-comedy.

Below you’ll find more details on my recommendations this week, followed by a full list of all the new movies heading to streaming services this week. We also have a guide to the top TV shows you can watch in the coming days.

I finally got to see “You Can See Everything” over the weekend (thanks to its delayed international rollout). And even with high expectations because of the incredible word-of-mouth I’d seen on social media for weeks, it still blew me away. It’s being touted as one of the year’s best movies, and holds a 97% score on Rotten Tomatoes, with an equally strong viewer rating of 95%. A shoo-in for awards season, it's one of 2026's most buzzy new releases.

Take it from me: This is a doc where the less you know before watching, the better. So, to avoid spoiling anything, I’ll keep the following outline vague. Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it follows the infamous fraudster Elizabeth Holmes 34 days before she’s due to be sent to prison. Holmes allows a film crew to document her daily life, but what starts as a simple documentary warps into something significantly more complex.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 24

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Starring Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis, it follows a quartet of promising young football players who park their athletic dreams to enlist in the United States Marine Corps during WWII. On the front lines, they face numerous hardships but also participate in a football game that became known as “The Mosquito Bowl” ahead of the Battle of Okinawa. Which, for a moment, let these troops forget the horrors of war.

“The Way of the Warrior Kid” so closely resembles “The Karate Kid” that I half-wonder if it’s legally actionable. The inspiration for Apple’s new coming-of-age drama movie is so clear that even the title doesn’t try to hide it. But imitation is the sincerest form of flattery. I can’t say this Apple original looks like a critical darling-in-waiting, but hopefully it’ll offer some feel-good fun. And surely it can’t be received worse than the 2010 “Karate Kid” reboot, right?

Chris Pratt stars as Uncle Jake, a US Navy SEAL staying with his older sister, Sarah (Linda Cardellini), over the summer after being injured in the line of duty. Taking his nephew, Marc (Jude Hill), under his wing, Jake resolves to help him learn to stand up for himself against a pack of school-year bullies. Cue the epic training montage and scenes of family bonding.

I’ve got a personal reason to recommend “The Magic Faraway Tree.” The original Enid Blyton books were a childhood favorite, so seeing characters like Moonface (Nonso Anozie) and Saucepan Man (Dustin Demri-Burns) on the big screen transported me to a simpler time. The fantasy adventure is a whimsical ride, and clearly made with younger viewers in mind. Grown-ups might find it a little too simplistic, but if you’ve got young kids, I bet they’ll love it. Just don’t blame me if they want to watch it on repeat for weeks.

Starring Andrew Garfield, Claire Foy, Nicola Coughlan and Rebecca Ferguson (who’s deliciously wicked as the villain, Dame Snap), “The Magic Faraway Tree” sees a family move from the big city to the countryside in hopes of a simpler, technology-free life. Once in their new digs, the family’s three children discover a magical tree full of quirky inhabitants, and if that wasn’t exciting enough, the tree can also transport them to dazzling fantasy lands.

I can’t say that Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson would have been my first choice if you’d asked me to assemble a dream duo for a “buddy” action movie, but it’s a combination that works surprisingly well in practice. Which isn’t to say “Runner” is flawless; the plot is very pedestrian, but the action is entertaining, and Ritchson and Wilson’s dynamic is great.

Ritchson plays a former soldier, now working as a “runner,” essentially a courier for high-value items, both legal and illegal. Tasked with making a critical medical delivery, he reluctantly teams up with an unlikely ally, Wilson’s Ben Bishop. A young girl’s life hangs in the balance, and the job is complicated when the pair become the target of a criminal cartel. “Runner” is a fast-paced action-comedy, with a pair of likable leads. It’s disposable fun.

Rory is a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom’s Guide based in the UK. He covers a wide range of topics but with a particular focus on gaming and streaming. When he’s not reviewing the latest games, searching for hidden gems on Netflix, or writing hot takes on new gaming hardware, TV shows and movies, he can be found attending music festivals and getting far too emotionally invested in his favorite football team.

#3025. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. #3024. As Tech Stocks Crash, Is Berkshire Hathaway a Safe-Haven Investment?

Berkshire's stock has been rising while tech stocks have been falling.

By David Jagielski, CPA – Nov 23, 2026 at 4:59PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Although Warren Buffett no longer runs Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.49%)(BRKB +0.41%), the company still operates with the same investing principles, focusing its efforts on high-quality investments.

At a time when the markets have been shaky of late, particularly pertaining to the tech sector, Berkshire has been a stock that's been rising in value lately. Could it be a safe place for investors to park their money, amid the uncertainty in not only tech but also the broader markets?

Tech stocks have been doing well for the most part this year, as the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF has risen by around 13%, which is in line with Berkshire's performance -- it's up around 14%.

But what's notable is the shift over the past three months. Berkshire's stock has risen by 16% during that stretch, while the Tech-focused ETF has gone in the opposite direction, falling by 11%. It could be a sign of investors pivoting to safer stocks, such as Berkshire, in the wake of all the turmoil involving tech of late.

Berkshire is, after all, a prototypical value stock that doesn't take on much risk and which can provide investors with excellent value. However, under new CEO Greg Abel, I've noticed the company investing more in tech, including Bending Spoons, a serial acquirer I couldn't imagine Buffett investing in. But it is a minor position in the overall portfolio.

By and large, Berkshire's focus remains unchanged, with close to half of its portfolio centered around three large, iconic companies: Apple, American Express, and Coca-Cola.

With stalwarts such as those centering its portfolio, the stock can indeed be a safe option for investors. But whether it's the best option is certainly debatable.

There are a couple of reasons I wouldn't buy Berkshire's stock for safety. The first is that it doesn't pay a dividend, which can be crucial when investors want to maximize returns amid uncertainty. The second is that at 16 times earnings, the stock is a bit more expensive than normal.

Ultimately, with markets in a bit of a downturn of late, I think investors can find better options, such as discounted dividend stocks that at least offer decent yields. Berkshire can be a good safe-haven investment, but before buying the stock, investors may want to consider other options.

#3023. Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft announced two new AI models at Ignite 2026 that promise impressive performance for much lower cost. They could reshape its relationship with OpenAI and Anthropic for good.

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a company is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open issue.

The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

The single biggest shopping day of the year is almost here, and you’ve probably seen many offers claiming to be some of the best iPhone Black Friday deals around. But before you make an impulsive decision, it’s worth knowing which of the current models is actually worth your money.

The beauty of Apple’s current lineup is that it’s the most diverse it’s ever been, covering different form factors and budgets — so I’m pitting the iPhone 17, 17e, Air, 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo against each other. With Black Friday deals rolling out across major carriers and retailers, it’s pretty tricky determining which one of them is the right fit.

Having tested all of them, I’ll break down which iPhones are actually worth your money this Black Friday.

6.1-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,532 x 1,170)

Frankly, the iPhone 17e is the one I’d recommend buying the least. What makes it an even tougher sell is that it launched at $599 earlier this year, but has since been given a $100 price hike that brings it to $699. Despite that, the iPhone 17e remains the most affordable entry point into Apple’s current lineup if you’re buying unlocked without any carrier deals or bundles attached.

It covers the basics of what I’d want in a modern iPhone, like 256GB of starting storage, all-day battery life, speedy A19 performance, and a pocket-friendly build. Even though it runs iOS 27 just like all the others, it doesn’t make the cut for Siri AI — which is a bummer if you want a smarter, more proactive assistant. At the same time, it’s the only iPhone in the stable that is still stuck with a 60Hz refresh rate.

In terms of utility, you’re only getting a single 48MP main camera on the back — though I can’t overlook the fact that it performs well above average, including in low light. In fact, I was surprised in my iPhone 17e vs Pixel 10a face-off how its single rear camera held up.

But as I said at the beginning, I can’t recommend getting this one knowing that the next model in the lineup exists.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

If there’s one model in the lineup that hits the sweet spot for almost everyone, it’s the iPhone 17 — and yes, it too got a $100 price hike a couple of months back that now puts it at $899. Even with that increase, it’s easy for me to recommend for a number of reasons.

For that small jump over the iPhone 17e, you get a vastly smoother 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display, faster 35W wired and 25W MagSafe charging, and way better color options to choose from. Sure, it’s running the same A19 chip as the iPhone 17e, but its faster 120Hz refresh rate makes a huge difference in making UI animations look and feel smoother.

More importantly, the iPhone 17 delivers a far more satisfying camera experience. Pairing its 48MP main sensor with a dedicated 48MP ultrawide lens, this setup gives me more creative flexibility with my shots. I’ve broken down everything about them in my iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 17e face-off, which resulted in a lopsided win for the iPhone 17.

When it launched, I had so much excitement and buzz for the iPhone Air — until I actually started using it. As impressive as its 5.6mm titanium frame feels in the hand, the iPhone Air is another model that’s tough for me to recommend — especially now that Apple’s $100 price hike pushes its starting cost to a steep $1,099.

You’re paying a serious premium strictly for thinness, while getting less functionality compared to the rest of the group. It doesn’t help either that the iPhone 17 sits below it at $200 less.

The biggest trade-offs show up in daily use. Even though you get a gorgeous 6.5-inch 120Hz OLED display and speedy A19 Pro performance, its battery capacity is dramatically limited by its razor-thin profile — resulting in noticeably shorter battery life and slower charging than the rest of the lineup. Worse yet, it’s also stuck with just a single 48MP rear camera like the iPhone 17e. You don’t get an ultrawide lens, no macro shots, or definitely no telephoto zoom on a phone that costs $1,000-plus. We've even put its camera to the test against the iPhone 17e and I was shocked by how the iPhone Air barely came out on top.

Don’t get me wrong, I miss the days of thin and light phones, but when I’ve gotten accustomed to modern phones that pack dual cameras and easily get me through an 8-hour work shift without worrying about running out of juice, it’s so hard to go back to anything less.

Without question, I’d recommend looking out for Black Friday deals on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. If you want the best of what Apple makes, both the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro and $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max earn an easy recommendation from me. Yes, Apple hit both models with a $100 price hike this year and added a bit of heft — but they justify their premiums.

For starters, they’re packing a blazing-fast A20 Pro chip under the hood, offering access to the full Siri AI suite, and sporting a triple-48MP camera system headlined by a versatile new variable-aperture main lens.

No matter which one you end up getting, I love the fact that Apple still gave both phones identical camera hardware, 60W wired charging, and Pro Controls that make them more of a photographer’s camera. While the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max inherently has the bigger screen and battery, I personally find the smaller iPhone 18 Pro much easier to handle. Ultimately, choosing between them comes down purely to size preference.

Either way, you won’t question the decision to buy either one. And quite frankly, they’re well worth the cost over the iPhone Air.

Apple’s first foldable is easily the most exciting iPhone in years, and despite its steep $1,999 starting price, I still recommend buying it if you want a compact phone that unfolds into a mini tablet. Its sturdy titanium frame, nearly invisible crease, and nano-texture inner display, make it feel far more refined than a typical first-generation device.

Having a pocketable 5.4-inch outer screen is great for when I want to use it one-handed, and I also love how it opens into a 7.6-inch canvas unfolded with intuitive split-screen multitasking in iOS 27. Not only does its unique design make it perfect for creators who want to shoot videos of themselves by pairing the outer screen with the superior rear cameras, but it’s also an absolute powerhouse for everyday productivity — something none of the others can match to the same degree.

Of course, you still have to accept a few trade-offs compared to the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max. You’re giving up Face ID, a dedicated telephoto zoom lens, no variable aperture, and no Pro Controls, while some third-party apps still aren’t fully optimized for the wider inner display.

Even with those compromises, nothing else in Apple’s lineup matches the Duo’s versatility — and if you can soften the blow with a Black Friday trade-in deal, I don’t think you’ll regret the purchase.

When it comes to outdoor visibility, the iPhone Duo takes the crown with a blinding peak brightness of 2,558 nits. It’s an intriguing find because of its nano-texture display. While it’s still viewable outdoors, it lacks the contrast and vibrant color tones of the Pro models — with the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 18 Pro topping out at an impressive 2,326 nits and 2,314 nits, respectively.

Stepping down to the middle of the pack, the iPhone Air reached 1,678 nits, while the standard iPhone 17 hit 1,505 nits. I think both are plenty bright for everyday outdoor use. Unsurprisingly, the iPhone 17e trails the entire group at 1,002 nits.

3DMark Wild Life Original Unlimited (score/fps)

Our benchmark testing draws a clear line between Apple’s A19-powered models and the newer A20 Pro flagships. The iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo all run on the A20 Pro chip — and, as a result, deliver class-leading CPU speeds, with Geekbench 6 scores clustering tightly around 4,700 single-core and 12,700 multi-core.

On the graphics front, the iPhone 18 Pro edges out the pack in 3DMark Wild Life Original Unlimited with a score of 38,667, just ahead of the 18 Pro Max at 38,474 and the Duo at 36,515.

Meanwhile, the A19-equipped iPhone 17e and iPhone 17 trail noticeably behind in both CPU and GPU performance, while the A19 Pro inside the iPhone Air offers only a slight uptick over the standard 17. Even so, all three handle everyday apps effortlessly.

If battery endurance is important to you, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max truly separate themselves from the rest of the pack. In our battery test, the iPhone 18 Pro Max led the way with an average of 18 hours and 27 minutes, while the smaller iPhone 18 Pro wasn’t far behind at 16 hours and 17 minutes.

Meanwhile, the rest of the lineup clusters tightly around the 12.5- to 13.5-hour mark. The iPhone Duo edges out the non-Pro models at an average of 13 hours and 20 minutes, while the iPhone 17 and iPhone Air came in at over 12 hours.

At the end of the day, I recommend looking out for Black Friday deals on the iPhone 17, iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Duo. While the iPhone 17 is a great entry point for everyday users and the iPhone Duo delivers unmatched foldable versatility, the iPhone 18 Pro takes the crown as the best overall balance and value of the bunch.

You get the exact same blazing-fast A20 Pro performance, variable-aperture triple-camera system, and speedy 60W charging as the pricier iPhone 18 Pro Max — all in a much easier-to-handle size that saves you $100 upfront. Unless you specifically crave a massive screen or a folding display, the iPhone 18 Pro is the one I’d look out for Black Friday.

#3020. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft could reshape enterprise spending, but there's a critical difference between estimated value and money saved.

We all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026

I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:

This means the company doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

#3019. Are We There Yet? NASA’s Escapade Is Heading to Mars in a ‘Pioneering’ Maneuver

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

No space agency has ever staged spacecraft in orbit for a year before sending them on to Mars.

NASA launched its Escapade mission just over a year ago to send two spacecraft, nicknamed Blue and Gold, to Mars. After spending a year looping near Earth, the twin probes completed a gravity-assist maneuver this month and are now en route to the red planet.

It’s an exciting time for NASA. Blue and Gold, named for the school colors of UC Berkeley where they were built, completed the agency’s first powered Earth flyby.

Typically, spacecraft use a planet’s or the sun’s gravity to get close to the planet before slingshotting off into the distance. A notable example is Voyager 1, which used unpowered gravity-assisted flybys to reach the speeds needed to cross the light-day threshold earlier this week. Escapade did this with Earth’s gravity but also used thrusters to generate even more speed. Since there are two of them, NASA personnel had to perform this maneuver twice.

The other big win for NASA is that Mars will soon have two additional satellites in orbit to measure the planet’s magnetosphere, which is believed to have been stripped by the solar wind eons ago, when the planet likely had liquid water.

These satellites are notable for being NASA’s first low-cost mission to Mars, costing the agency approximately $75 million as part of the Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration program. It also marked the debut of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket for a space mission, and the company was able to achieve the first vertical landing of its rocket after sending Escapade on its way.

Escapade still has a long way to go. Blue and Gold are now spending the next 10 months flying into outer space. Their new trajectory is set to take them into Mars’ orbital path, timed in such a way that the twin satellites will arrive at the same time that Mars naturally shows up, allowing the red planet to capture the twins in its orbit as it flies by. NASA says that both are set to arrive at Mars by early September next year.

By the time the twins get there, they will have been in space for 22 months. Flights to Mars require months of deep space travel, impeccable timing and loads of fuel. However, if missions hit specific launch windows, they require far less fuel.

This is a well-documented maneuver known as the Hohmann Transfer, and NASA’s JPL has a neat math exercise to show how it’s calculated. NASA intentionally launched Escapade a year early so that the satellites could hang out in a gravitational sweet spot called the L2 Earth-Sun Lagrange point. This is a point in space on the side of the Earth opposite the sun, and the idea was to have the spacecraft already in orbit and ready for the next Mars launch window.

Once it opened, the satellites engaged their thrusters, performed a gravity-assisted flyby of Earth to gain speed, and launched themselves into outer space.

The tactic of sending Escapade to the L2 Lagrange point to wait for a Mars window to open is arguably NASA’s biggest win, as no space agency has ever attempted it. The benefit is that it allows agencies to launch payloads into orbit bound for Mars whenever they have the time, then use Earth gravity assists to slingshot them out to Mars when it’s most efficient.

“With this loiter orbit and Earth flyby, Escapade is pioneering a new strategy for getting to Mars,” Jeff Parker, CTO of Advanced Space and lead mission designer, said in a statement. “This method provides the flexibility to launch almost anytime and then use Earth’s gravity to get a boost to Mars, rather than waiting every two years to launch there directly when the planets are aligned.”

The maneuver paid dividends. JAXA, Japan’s national space agency, launched its MMX spacecraft on Oct. 20, which is within the current Mars launch window and employs the same Hohmann Transfer method to get to Mars. The spacecraft is headed to Phobos and Deimos, Mars’s moons.

Despite using the more traditional method of waiting for the window to open to launch, JAXA’s MMX is slated to reach its destination in August next year, just a couple of weeks ahead of Escapade. When you factor in that Escapade performed its gravity-assist slingshot on Nov. 9, roughly two weeks before MMX launched, the spacecraft will reach their respective destinations in approximately the same amount of time, validating NASA’s trajectory strategy.
