#2950. SpaceX Sued by 2 States Over Grok’s Sexualized Images of Women and Children

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

People used Grok to generate millions of "spicy mode" images.

Oregon and Virginia on Monday filed lawsuits against SpaceX, alleging that Elon Musk’s company violated consumer protection laws, months after people used Grok Imagine to generate millions of sexualized images of women and children.

Grok Imagine is an image- and video-generation tool developed by SpaceXSI, a division of SpaceX. Shortly after launching last summer, the tool added a “spicy mode,” which enabled people to generate images and videos showing partial nudity and adult-themed videos. Grok Imagine is integrated into Grok, which is Musk’s AI chatbot.

In the lawsuits, separate but jointly filed, Virginia and Oregon allege that the sexualized images — including child sexual abuse material — were generated without the knowledge and consent of the women and children shown in the images and videos.

Read more: After Rampant AI-Powered Abuse, Grok Doubles Down

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in a press release that SpaceX misled people into thinking that their images and data would be safe.

“When xAI [now renamed SpaceXSI] allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

Donna Rice Hughes, CEO of child internet safety organization Enough Is Enough, praised Oregon and Virginia for taking action against SpaceX.

“It is abhorrent that women and children are preyed upon in this manner and even more repugnant that xAI’s Grok ‘spicy mode’ has not kept up with bad actors who abuse their terms of service,” Hughes told CNET, adding that Musk’s “team can find ways to prevent criminal misuse of Grok, and at the very least, disable Grok’s ‘spicy mode.'”

Grok Imagine launched on Aug. 5, 2025, and within months, it was used to generate millions of sexualized images, which were posted on the social media platform X, which is also owned by Musk’s SpaceX.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield alleged SpaceX “knowingly designed” Grok Imagine and promoted spicy mode’s lack of safeguards as a feature, not a bug.

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material,” Rayfield said in a statement. “The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”

During a 9-day span starting in late December, Grok posted about 3 million sexualized images, according to an analysis from the Center for Countering Digital Hate.

In a statement posted Monday on X, SpaceX said that people using Grok to generate sexualized images and videos violated the platform’s terms of service and worked “aggressively to circumvent our safeguards.” The company said it tightened protections after the misuse and continues to test and adjust them as needed. SpaceX also said it notifies law enforcement authorities “when someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content.”

Earlier this year, several minor Jane Does filed a proposed class action lawsuit against xAI after people used their photos to generate child sexual abuse material using Grok via spicy mode. That case is still ongoing.

In July, a victim’s family also filed suit after photographer Russell Bloodworth in Arkansas allegedly used spicy mode to generate explicit photos of children. xAI went on the offensive, suing Bloodworth and South Carolina man Terry Wayne Harwood, who is also accused of using Grok to generate child sexual abuse material. The company seeks damages for expenses incurred in fighting lawsuits and for reputational harm.

SpaceX and xAI have faced lawsuits for other things aside from illicit image generation. The companies were sued for allegedly sharing sensitive data and for allegedly causing users to be hospitalized for psychosis after harmful chat conversations on Grok.

Monday’s lawsuits against SpaceX are among nearly 400 cases brought against 129 AI companies in the US, according to the AI Lawsuit Tracker. Many Big Tech companies have been sued for allegedly harming the mental health of adults and children. In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a lawsuit brought by US states alleging the company intentionally designed Instagram and other platforms to be addictive to children.

Companies such as ByteDance — owner of TikTok — Snap, Google and others face more than 2,400 federal lawsuits alleging that their platforms harm the mental health of children.

#2949. Uber Riders Can Now Request to Have Their Trips Recorded

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

In four cities, Uber riders can request rides with drivers who use the Record My Ride feature.

Starting this week, Uber riders in select markets will be able to specify that they want their trip recorded on video. The feature, which is being introduced in Baltimore, Indianapolis, St. Louis, and Raleigh, North Carolina, adds a new Recorded Rides choice to the app alongside other familiar ride options like UberX and UberXL. Uber says that the new feature gives “greater confidence that a recording will be there if something doesn’t go as planned.”

After a series of rider safety investigations and sexual assault lawsuit settlements, Uber began looking for ways to boost passenger safety and confidence in the service. The ridesharing platform first tested in-app trip audio recording in late 2019, then piloted the Record My Ride feature in 2022, before finally rolling out the video recording function in earnest, first in San Francisco in 2023, then nationally across the US in 2024.

According to Uber, the knowledge that a trip is being recorded gives both riders and drivers peace of mind.

While drivers can opt out of using the feature in their settings, more than half of its active drivers in the US choose to record their trips in the Record My Ride feature.

Starting this week, Uber riders in those four cities will be able to request a recorded ride during the hailing process in the Uber app and, when possible, be automatically matched with a driver using the feature. Choosing a recorded ride doesn’t affect the fare.

Record My Ride has been available to Uber’s drivers, though not passengers, for a few years now. The feature uses the front-facing camera on the driver’s phone to capture trip audio and video.

“Uber can only review recordings uploaded as part of a safety report or insurance claim,” a representative told CNET.

Not selecting a Recorded Ride doesn’t guarantee that your trip won’t be recorded in some way. Many Uber drivers choose to install separate dash cams in their vehicles, often with multiple cameras recording into the cabin. Uber offers drivers the option to register their dash cam with the service, but this is separate from the pilot.

“Drivers can use a separate dash cam, provided they comply with local laws,” an Uber representative told CNET in an email, “but Recorded Rides specifically matches riders with drivers recording through Record My Ride.”

Uber says it’s exploring additional ways to use recordings to keep its riders and drivers safe. It will soon begin proactively activating the Record My Ride feature on drivers’ devices during trips that may benefit from additional oversight, such as late-night or trips involving teenagers. Uber is also looking into automatically turning on video recordings “when trips are not proceeding as expected,” such as when a trip goes significantly off the projected course or if a crash is detected.

Uber says it’s also looking into testing the automatic activation of audio recording on riders’ phones during nighttime trips. Passengers would have to consent to this, which would require the app to use their phone’s microphone.

TL;DR: Surging tech stocks aren't great news for bonds, or for mortgage rates.

Mortgage rates have had some substantial day-over-day swings lately, and today, unfortunately it's an upward swing.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.38% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points higher than yesterday and four basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Recently news about big tech has often pulled rates down. Investor concerns about AI profitability keep cropping up, and when they do, tech stocks and bonds lose their appeal and Treasuries have been picking up the slack. Mortgage rates are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury, and Treasury prices and yields move inversely. More demand for the 10YT drives prices up, and sends yields (and thus, mortgage rates) down.

Today's the opposite, though. Investors are having a bout of tech exuberance as Jensen Huang got reinstated as Nvidia CEO, and lots of excitement about tech stocks and bonds means less enthusiasm for Treasuries.

Here's the thing, though: Markets are fickle. They also move fast. And they aren't the only influence on mortgage rates.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Lately, we've seen two narratives influencing mortgage rates battling it out; depending on which one's stronger, daily rates move higher or lower. Up top I talked about how shifting perceptions of big tech have been driving mortgage rates (and yes, today, pushing them higher, though usually it's pulled rates down.) When rates are moving higher, more often it's been thanks to inflation — and while it's a lightweight work week, we're about to get heavyweight inflation news.

The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely.

The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation, so you can guess how things are likely to go at the Fed's December meeting. Markets already feel fairly certain about a quarter-percent rate hike.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out Wednesday morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

And speaking of: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

P.S.: I don't have to ask if anyone's playing Grand Theft Auto 'cause c'mon, of course. But did anyone else perk up when Lu asked about home loans? Yeah, that was probably just me. Jason and Lucia would have to change a lot about their lifestyle to qualify (we know they're working on building credit, but having all your income be cash you can't really document is not going to work for a lender). But hey, I'm rooting for them.

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.88% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

#2947. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2946. Nvidia's Stock Surges More Than 30% on Jensen Huang's Return. Will It Get Back to $200?

On Monday, the company announced that Huang is back as CEO, after resigning just a few weeks earlier.

By David Jagielski, CPA – Nov 23, 2026 at 6:40PM EST

What a turnaround. In just a single day, Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) stock jumped more than 30%. The tech company announced that it was reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, who had resigned earlier in the month after multiple extramarital affairs came to light. It also comes after the board said it wasn't considering bringing him back.

Investors emphatically gave the move their stamp of approval, with the stock skyrocketing on the day, back to around a $4 trillion valuation. It is, however, still down more than 30% from its peak. Given the excitement around Nvidia's stock right now, could it be heading back to $200?

With the huge rally on Monday, Nvidia's stock is back up to around the levels it was at a few weeks ago, when Huang initially resigned. However, even before the scandal came to light, the stock was already falling from its highs; a month ago, the tech stock was trading at around $210.

The company's board initially said it would not take Huang back as CEO. However, by Monday, it unanimously voted to reinstate him. A big part of the reason appears to be due to the government's input. U.S. President Donald Trump has spoken positively of Huang and believed it was in the company's best interests to have him back, and says he convinced the board to take him back, saying, "I made the deal."

While there's one less question mark around Nvidia's business right now, there are still others looming, including what will happen involving Congress. Huang is scheduled to meet with Congress on Dec. 1, facing questions about a relationship with a possible Chinese spy.

Trump, however, says he gave Nvidia's board assurances about national security: "We gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot." On the surface, it would appear that issues relating to national security may not be significant enough to warrant any further concern from the company's board.

Given how volatile the stock has been and the excitement around it, I wouldn't be surprised to see Nvidia shares get back up to $200 in the near future. However, the broader market risk of rising interest rates still looms, which could impact the business and its growth prospects in the longer run.

For now, the market appears to be focused on the short term; however, this can expose the stock to significant volatility. Investors should tread carefully because while Nvidia's hot today, if market sentiment sours next month due to rising interest rates, things could change quickly.

#2945. The Midterms Put Data Center Permitting Back in Play. Here Are 2 Industrial Stocks That Win if Power Moves Behind the Meter.

Bloom Energy and Caterpillar have sold off sharply along with the AI sector, but shifting electricity trends could support long-term business success.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 23, 2026 at 7:11PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Bloom Energy ›

Artificial intelligence (AI) is likely to be a world-changing technology, but it uses a huge amount of electricity. AI power demand has been so high that it has driven up electricity costs for everyone, hitting the pocketbooks of everyday people even as inflation is running hot. That's resulted in pushback, with data centers playing a prominent role in the recent midterm elections. That could actually be a net positive for companies like Bloom Energy (BE +18.09%) and Caterpillar (CAT +7.17%). Here's why.

The current administration in Washington has been very supportive of artificial intelligence. With the House and Senate changing hands next year following big wins in November's election, support for AI could waver. There are already states that have put up roadblocks to further data center construction. One of the biggest problems is electricity, with a push for data centers to supply their own power to avoid straining the grid.

That, however, could be a huge win for companies like Bloom Energy and Caterpillar. Bloom Energy makes factory-built hydrogen fuel cells that can be easily deployed where they are needed to provide off-grid power. Caterpillar is best known for making the heavy construction equipment used to build data centers, but it also makes generators used to provide off-grid power.

If data centers have to bring their own power, Bloom Energy and Cat are primed to help. Notably, Bloom Energy entered 2026 with a $6 billion product backlog, up 140% year over year. That backlog has likely grown throughout the year (it only reports its backlog annually) and could get even bigger in the future. The company, which has lost money for years, is likely to turn profitable in 2026.

Caterpillar ended the third quarter with a record $78 billion backlog, up 96% year over year. While not all of that backlog is tied to its power systems, the bigger takeaway is that demand remains very strong across all its products. That said, management noted that bringing up manufacturing capacity in its power division remains a primary goal because demand is so strong.

The shifting political winds in Washington could increase the already strong demand that Bloom Energy and Cat are seeing. But investors need to distinguish between the stocks and the businesses here. AI-related stocks, including both of these companies, have been volatile of late. If you own them or are considering buying them, you need to approach them with a long-term mindset. Another option is to add them to your wish list and be ready to pounce if there is a deep AI-driven bear market.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

For a while this morning, Anthropic (ANT -1.43%) looked like it would soar today after news of Jensen Huang's dramatic return to Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) broke. Shares of the newly public company opened up 5.4%.

But by the closing bell, Anthropic was down 1.4%. Not a bad day per se, but consider the gains from the rest of the tech market:

Just two trading days after its debut, in what was the year's biggest gain for the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +6.51%), Anthropic stock inched lower. Why did the Claude maker's stock miss out on most of the marketwide rally?

Nvidia's board announced this morning that it was bringing Huang back as CEO, president, and board member. That's just under a week after Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that Huang's return was not on the table. The official announcement said that the board had "received input from senior levels of the United States government," giving it confidence that "Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

The government input was, in fact, from the most senior of senior levels: the U.S. President. Trump told CNBC that he spoke with the board "directly and indirectly" to advocate for Huang's return: "I convinced them." Trump reassured the board that he did not pose a national security threat after Attorney General Todd Blanche assured the President that investigators had no evidence to suggest wrongdoing.

Whatever the full reasoning behind that led to the board's decision, the move -- a shock to many -- breathed life into an ailing AI trade that was in serious need of good news; the Nasdaq  turned red for 2026 on Friday after entering a correction earlier in the month.

A few reasons: first, Reuters reported that President Trump -- Vice President JD Vance, too -- intervened in part because they saw Huang as crucial to keeping American companies competitive in open-weight AI -- a market in which China leads.

Open-weight models are offered to the public -- often for free -- to download, tweak, adapt, and run however and wherever they see fit.

That stands in stark contrast to the closed models of Anthropic and rival OpenAI, which offer comparatively little in the way of customization and, most importantly, run in the cloud and can only be accessed through the company. That ensures they get paid every time you use their models. To state the obvious, they do not get paid if a company opts for an open-weight model. That makes them a potential threat to Anthropic's growth -- a pretty substantial one.

Nvidia, on the other hand, gets paid no matter what models get used, so long as the servers powering the model use its chips. More open-weight models mean more potential customers. That's why Jensen Huang has been an advocate, making several major investments in open-weight developers.

Whether or not Huang is at the helm, open-weight models pose a genuine threat to Anthropic's business. It is one of the core reasons I would avoid the stock. At the moment, Anthropic's moat -- the thing keeping customers paying Anthropic and not its competitors -- comes almost entirely from having the best models.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

That's not a very strong one in my opinion, and over time, I see Anthropic struggling to keep customers from switching workloads over to cheaper open-weight alternatives.

#2943. I Rate Buy Now, Pay Later Apps; Here’s My Holiday Advice

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

“Buy now, pay later” can help stretch your holiday budget further, but pick your BNPL app carefully and avoid loan stacking.

Head of Content, Personal & Student Loans

As Americans compile their shopping lists ahead of the holiday season, I’ve been compiling my own kind of list — a list of 25 data points, gathered across six “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) apps, fed into a rubric of five categories and 22 subcategories, to produce a star rating for each app.

It’s a big list. I check it twice (or 10 times).

By the end, I know more about these apps than anyone should, and I’m eager to bestow my knowledge on the next unsuspecting person who utters “Klarna” in my vicinity.

I should have plenty of opportunities this year. Nearly 2 in 5 holiday spenders (38%) plan to use BNPL, according to NerdWallet’s holiday spending report. Concerningly, the same report found that a higher share of BNPL users expect they won’t be able to make their payments in full and on time compared to credit card users.

Using BNPL for holiday shopping isn’t inherently bad, but there are risks, including sneaky fees and the ease of loan stacking across many providers.

Here’s how to minimize those risks and set yourself up for success this holiday season.

Brenton Harrison, a certified financial planner in Nashville, says many of his clients are turning to buy now, pay later in the “messy middle of life,” when everyday expenses are high and budgets are tight. This is especially true during the holidays.

“They have kids they're providing for, or they’re trying to go travel and see family,” Harrison says. “When those expenses pile up, it can be very attractive to be able to spread out payments.”

Since BNPL divides your total purchase into smaller installments, typically due every two weeks, it feels easier on your cash flow than having to pay all at once.

While Harrison is open to his clients using BNPL, he emphasizes how important it is to understand the terms before opting in. BNPL apps only require a soft credit pull and a short application. When you can apply for a loan in just a few clicks, it’s easy to miss when payments are due or whether they’ll include interest.

But if clients understand the terms and are certain they can make the payments, Harrison says BNPL's set repayment schedule can be a better option than more open-ended financing.

“With a credit card, [a holiday purchase] might be something that they buy over and over and over again, because that interest just continues to accrue over time, and they never pay it off,” he says.

Not all BNPL apps are created equal. I measure the top apps across multiple categories, but I weigh affordability the highest. My thinking is if you’re already strapped for cash, it’s a bad idea to pay extra just to break up the payments.

There are providers, like Affirm and PayPal, that don’t charge interest with a common pay-in-four term (your total purchase, divided into four installments). They also charge no fees, including no late fees for missed payments.

Compare that to apps, like Sezzle and Zip, that may charge an automatic service or origination fee with your first installment, as well as late fees.

Long-term BNPL financing, which can stretch months or even years, usually includes interest, expressed as an annual percentage rate or APR. This is a more expensive payment option than a zero-interest pay-in-four.

Pay close attention to your checkout screen to see what you’re offered. Are the installment amounts equal or is the first installment higher than the others? That may mean there’s a fee. Do you see an APR listed? That means you’re paying interest.

Harrison points out that just because a store partners with a BNPL company doesn’t mean that’s your only option. Download a different BNPL app, search for the store and see if you get access to better terms, like a 0% offer.

Taking out multiple loans with different BNPL providers is known as “loan stacking,” and it’s risky.

Because you’re juggling different payment amounts due on different days, it’s hard to keep track of what’s coming out of your bank account. This is especially true if you set up automatic payments, which most BNPL apps require. If you overdraw your checking account, your bank will likely charge a fee.

According to research published in August by the Federal Reserve, 11% percent of BNPL users had a BNPL payment trigger an overdraft or nonsufficient funds fee from their bank in the prior year. People with less savings were even more likely to pay fees.

Before applying for multiple BNPL loans, look at a typical month of expenses and ask if there’s extra room in your budget for those payments, Harrison says.

“If you’re just assuming that because you’re spreading it out that you’ll be able to pay it, that's where I think people can get in trouble,” he says. “They set it and forget it, and they don't realize, ‘Oh, I am in no better position to pay that next month than I am this month, or I have three of these going at the same time, and collectively, it's more than I can manage.’”

Most apps send payment reminders, so you can potentially reschedule the payment or change your payment method.

Still, it’s best to avoid the headache to begin with. If you’re feeling pressured to spend more this holiday season, communicate your limits clearly with loved ones, Harrison says, and avoid any loans you can’t comfortably repay.

“Think about the purchase itself, especially around the holidays,” he says. “There's a big difference between something that I can pay off over three months and something that I should have never been buying in the first place.”

#2942. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

The new cards offer perks like faster paths to status and elevated earning rates when purchasing tickets with partners.

Etihad Guest, the loyalty program of Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways, is expanding its U.S. presence by introducing two new credit cards. Most people won’t get much value from these cards, but they can make sense for Etihad frequent flyers who want elite status.

The two cards are the Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card ($99 annual fee) and the Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card ($499 annual fee). Issued by the First National Bank of Omaha, both offer faster pathways to earning and maintaining elite status and the ability to earn extra miles on Etihad purchases.

They also offer extra miles on international transactions (neither has foreign transaction fees) and purchases with Etihad’s partner airlines, which include U.S. carriers like American Airlines and JetBlue Airways.

Here’s what you need to know about the cards.

The Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card comes with a $99 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the card is offering the following welcome offer for new applicants: Earn up to 40,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 10,000 miles after the first purchase and an additional 30,000 miles after spending $3,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: You’ll also get Etihad Silver status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account. Unlike most airlines, that entry-level status is enough to get you into the business class lounge when traveling through Etihad’s hub at Abu Dhabi’s Zayed International Airport.

You can retain that status by spending $20,000 a year on the card, or $3,000 a year on Etihad purchases.

The Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card comes with a $499 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

5 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

The only differences in rewards between the premium and standard cards are increased earning rates for eligible airline purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the premium card offers a higher welcome offer compared to the standard card: Earn up to 60,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 20,000 miles after the first purchase and 40,000 miles after spending $7,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: The premium card offers a faster track to elite status: automatic Silver status upon card approval and Gold status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account.

To maintain Gold status, you’ll need to spend $40,000 a year on the card, or $8,000 on Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you’ll have Silver status.

Wi-Fi benefit: After your first Etihad purchase, you’ll get 3,000 Etihad Guest miles, enough to cover Wi-Fi costs on a long-haul Etihad flight. You’ll then get those miles again after each cardholder anniversary.

Travel benefits: The card offers a statement credit for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck and select travel protections. If you already have a premium travel card, you might already have access to these perks.

The card also includes a Priority Pass lounge access membership. However, an Etihad spokesperson told NerdWallet that it’s the entry-level membership tier, so you’ll need to pay for yourself and guests each time you visit a Priority Pass lounge. Most premium credit cards in the U.S. that offer Priority Pass allow complimentary visits for at least the cardholder.

The Etihad cards make the most sense for Etihad’s frequent flyers who are flying to or connecting through Abu Dhabi several times a year.

That’s because the standard card’s accelerated pathway to Etihad Guest’s Silver status tier can unlock the ability to choose business class lounge access in Abu Dhabi as a status perk.

With the premium card, you get a fast track to Gold. If you select lounge access as a Gold status perk, you can not only bring a guest on the same flight into the lounge, but also access Etihad’s worldwide lounge network. That includes Etihad’s own lounges in New York and Washington, D.C., as well as most partner lounges at other Etihad destinations.

Bear in mind that while Etihad has many partnerships with other airlines, it’s not part of an alliance, so you don’t get lounge benefits when traveling on partners. You’ll need to be flying on an Etihad-operated flight to get into the lounge.

If you primarily fly with other carriers, then Etihad status will have limited upside for you.

However, the Priority Pass lounge membership that comes with the premium card does not have that restriction. You can access Priority Pass lounges while flying on any airline, although you’ll need to pay an additional per-person $35 fee each visit.

The earning rates on the Etihad cards are lackluster for everyday spenders. The bonus categories are for airline purchases with Etihad and its partners, as well as international spending.

That means your day-to-day purchases at home, like groceries, dining out and gas, earn only 1 mile per $1 spent.

Plus, there are more ways to earn Etihad Guest miles than spending on an Etihad credit card. For example, you can transfer points to Etihad Guest from Bilt Rewards, Capital One and Citi ThankYou.

Those programs offer cards that typically have better benefits and bonus categories, and they offer flexibility on how you can use your points and miles. With an Etihad card, you can only earn Etihad Guest miles, which expire after 18 months without qualifying flight activity. (If you’re not traveling on Etihad or its partners at least once every 18 months, then you definitely should not get the cards.)

One of the most interesting perks of the new cards is the bonus category for spending with Etihad partner airlines — 2 miles per $1 for the standard card and 3 miles per $1 for the premium version. Typically, airline credit cards reward customers only for spending on the airline, not partners.

There are better cards available, though. Some offer as many or even more points per $1 on flights purchased directly from airlines.

If you want the card solely to earn more Etihad Guest miles, then the answer for most people is no.

While you can earn more miles for purchases with Etihad and partner airlines, the earning rates aren’t attractive enough to justify the annual fees, especially when compared with existing cards with currencies that transfer to Etihad Guest.

Status chasers could benefit from the fast track to elite status — but you would need to be a fairly frequent Etihad flyer to really take advantage of your elite benefits.

#2940. If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Best Move Investors Should Make

With stock market valuations approaching historic extremes, Warren Buffett's investing advice offers a simple strategy for navigating a potential bubble.

By Adam Spatacco – Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

Despite stubborn inflation, rising interest rates, geopolitical conflicts, and considerable economic uncertainty, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.73%), Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +6.51%), and Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +3.01%) have delivered impressive returns over the last four years. However, this rapid appreciation of stocks has also raised concerns that a bubble could be forming.

Those fears are intensifying as artificial intelligence (AI) stocks retreat from record highs. Both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 recently entered correction territory, although both indexes are rebounding sharply as Jensen Huang returns to the CEO position of Nvidia.

Fortunately, legendary investor Warren Buffett has a simple strategy for navigating periods of market turbulence.

Between Nov. 30, 2022 -- the day ChatGPT was launched to the public -- and Nov. 20, 2026, the S&P 500 advanced approximately 69%, equivalent to an annualized gain of roughly 14%. The Nasdaq performed even better, climbing roughly 97%, or 18% annually.

Much of this growth was driven by the AI revolution. Companies designing AI chips, providing cloud infrastructure, and building enterprise software have attracted outsize interest from growth investors. Meanwhile, demand for data centers is creating opportunities throughout the economy. Utilities, energy producers, industrial equipment manufacturers, and construction companies are increasingly benefiting from the infrastructure spending required to support AI adoption.

However, enthusiasm surrounding AI is also pushing stock market valuations toward historically expensive levels. One revealing indicator is the Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio, which measures the S&P 500's price relative to its average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last 10 years.

Unlike a traditional price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, CAPE readings smooth out short-term fluctuations in earnings. This makes it useful for assessing long-term valuations. Historically, the metric has averaged 17.7, meaning investors have generally paid around $18 for every dollar of normalized earnings.

Currently, the CAPE ratio sits around 41 -- dangerously close to its highest level in history. That places valuations at more than twice their historical average and well above the threshold that has occasionally preceded major market drawdowns.

For perspective, the CAPE ratio exceeded 30 before the 1929 stock market crash. During this period, the Dow plunged 89% through 1932. Meanwhile, the CAPE ratio reached an all-time high of 44 during the dot-com era. Once the bubble burst, the Nasdaq collapsed 77% between March 2000 and October 2002 while the S&P 500 declined approximately 49%.

These examples underscore why elevated valuations deserve attention. With that said, the CAPE ratio is not a reliable indicator of what the market will do in the near term. Moreover, readings between 30 and 40 do not automatically mean a crash is imminent. Rather, elevated CAPE ratios have historically been associated with subdued returns in the immediate years following a crash.

Although bubbles can produce stomach-churning losses in the short term, history demonstrates the resilience of the stock market. The S&P 500 has endured the Great Depression, multiple recessions, wars, financial crises, and numerous presidential administrations while continuing to generate long-term wealth.

Consider what happened to investors who bought stocks right at the height of the dot-com bubble. The Nasdaq peaked at approximately 5,048 in March 2000 before collapsing nearly 77% over the following two and a half years. Nevertheless, the index eventually recovered and surpassed its previous record in 2015.

As of this writing (Nov. 23), the Nasdaq stands near 24,142, representing 386% appreciation from its dot-com era peak. That's respectable even for someone who invested at one of the worst possible moments in modern market history.

The S&P 500 tells a similar story. Its March 2000 peak was 1,527, compared with roughly 7,224 as of this writing. That represents a gain of 375% despite the dot-com collapse, the 2008 financial crisis, and the COVID-19 crash.

The lesson here is straightforward: Even investors who bought stocks at historically expensive valuations eventually generated multibagger gains by remaining invested.

In Berkshire Hathaway's shareholder letter from 2016, Buffett acknowledged that market declines were inevitable. But the "Oracle of Omaha" also emphasized that no one can reliably forecast when they will occur. Buffett observed:

Buffett's investment philosophy emphasizes remaining invested in productive businesses rather than repeatedly moving between stocks and cash based on market predictions. Investors who sell during downturns face two difficult decisions: determining when to exit and deciding when to reinvest.

Getting either decision wrong often has consequences. Stock market recoveries tend to begin when economic conditions still appear bleak, meaning investors who wait for uncertainty to disappear end up missing out on gains.

For investors with a long-term time horizon, a prudent approach involves maintaining a diversified portfolio, holding an appropriate cash reserve, and continuing to invest through periods of volatility. Cash will provide the financial flexibility to buy the dip in quality companies when market sell-offs create compelling opportunities.

At the end of the day, building wealth requires staying invested through market volatility rather than trying to avoid every downturn.

#2939. What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Used-car dealers may charge you a reconditioning fee to cover their costs of getting cars ready for sale.

A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:

A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic issues that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit users are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

#2937. What Are Repositioning Cruises?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.

#2936. CFO Colette Kress Just Made This Subtle Shift That Could Save Nvidia Shareholders

Nvidia may now take a more deliberate approach to customer financing.

By Will Healy – Nov 23, 2026 at 8:06PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) continues to impress shareholders. Even though large companies tend to grow slowly, Nvidia has challenged that assertion by delivering triple-digit revenue growth, much as it did in the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended Oct. 25).

Unfortunately for shareholders, CEO Jensen Huang financed much of this growth through "circular financing," in which the company finances customers to sell products.

CFO Colette Kress, who was briefly interim CEO, questioned this strategy. She reined in much of this financial support for other companies' artificial intelligence (AI) projects. Assuming Huang follows her lead, here's how this approach could save Nvidia shareholders.

In recent months, investors have become more concerned about how Nvidia generated its revenue growth.

Nvidia was to provide financial backing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio. Huang wanted to backstop $250 billion of OpenAI purchases, but Kress stepped in to cut that commitment to $105 billion.

Although Kress has rejected the "circular financing" label, as interim CEO, she stated on the third-quarter 2027 earnings call that Nvidia would be "disciplined and selective" in its support for the neoclouds, which will likely reassure those investors who questioned Huang's prior approach.

This is critical for investors because analysts often view such financing as consistent with the end stage of a boom.

They have good reason to worry. Cisco Systems (CSCO +6.80%) was at the center of the dot-com boom when it backstopped several of its customers. In 2001, Cisco famously had to write down $2.25 billion in one quarter when several of the customers it backed declared bankruptcy. That write-down contributed to a stock price decline so profound that it took 26 years for its stock to return to its 2000 high.

With "everything Kress told us," the company carries around $118 billion in guarantees, several orders of magnitude higher than Cisco's write-down. Still, if projects fall behind schedule, the company will now revoke guarantees, a move that could shield it from painful write-offs later.

Moreover, Nvidia may not be vulnerable to a slump as severe as Cisco's. Nvidia's 18 P/E ratio as of Nov. 23 is a tiny fraction of the 222 P/E ratio that Cisco reached in early 2000, suggesting less downside if an AI bust occurs.

Furthermore, Kress's approach did not appear to meaningfully slow Nvidia, even in the short term. For fiscal Q4, it guided for $130 billion in revenue at the midpoint, a 91% year-over-year increase if that forecast holds. While that is slightly less than fiscal Q3's 103% revenue increase, it may be a small price to pay to mitigate the specter of massive write-downs later.

Kress's move to rein in customer financing could alleviate a significant worry about the stock, assuming Huang follows his advice now that he has returned as CEO.

Indeed, the possibility of bankruptcies among major customers leaves Nvidia financially exposed, and that vulnerability could hurt the stock.

Nonetheless, Kress's decision to be "disciplined and selective" about customer financing addresses a key concern with Nvidia's current business approach. While it may mean somewhat slower growth, the prospect of reduced financial exposure should an AI bust occur is likely a wise move in the long run.

#2924. 2 Asset Manager Stocks to Buy That Each Oversee More Than $1 Trillion

BlackRock and Blackstone offer buyers very different setups on growth, valuation, and risk.

By Rick Orford – Nov 23, 2026 at 8:38PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Blackstone ›

BlackRock (BLK +3.88%) and Blackstone (BX +4.57%) each oversee more than $1 trillion in assets, making them two of the largest asset management firms worldwide. But with one trading closer to its 52-week high and the other down sharply this year, the question is: Which stock offers the more attractive opportunity for buyers?

BlackRock offers exposure to one of the most diversified businesses in asset management. With $15.5 trillion in assets under management (AUM) at the end of the third quarter, up 15% from the previous year, the company has built an enormous platform spanning index funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and private markets.

On top of that, the company sees broad demand, attracting massive inflows across equities, fixed-income investments, alternative investments, and cash. For example, its iShares ETF business remains an important growth engine, while its active investment strategies attract capital from investors seeking opportunities beyond passive index investing.

Its third-quarter performance further strengthened the bull case in favor of the stock. Its third-quarter revenue rose 19% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 38%. Looking ahead, its ability to attract new money while expanding its technology and private markets businesses gives it several avenues for continued earnings growth.

The main drawback is valuation. So far this year, BlackRock stock is up about 5% and trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio based on estimated earnings performance of about 18, which means investors are paying about $18 for every $1 of expected earnings. That leaves less room for error if market conditions deteriorate or inflows slow down.

Another company has also built its business around alternative assets, giving investors exposure to private equity, real estate, and infrastructure.

Blackstone has also established itself as one of the biggest names in alternative-asset management, with $1.4 trillion in AUM as of the third quarter. More broadly, its latest results suggest that investor demand remains healthy despite a challenging backdrop for private markets. Specifically, the company attracted $63.3 billion in new money, bringing its trailing 12-month (TTM) inflows to $271.6 billion.

Beyond inflows, one encouraging development is the growth of its perpetual capital business, which reached $562 billion. These investment vehicles are designed to provide capital without the fixed fund life and fundraising cycles associated with traditional private equity funds. This gives Blackstone a larger pool of relatively stable capital that can support more predictable fee revenue over time.

Blackstone is also benefiting from several major investment themes, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), energy infrastructure, and private credit. After all, building data centers, expanding electricity capacity, and financing AI infrastructure requires enormous amounts of capital. And Blackstone has established investment platforms across all these themes, allowing it to participate in the biggest opportunities of the next decade.

Blackstone shares have fallen almost 27% this year, but that has made its valuation more reasonable, with the stock trading at a forward P/E of about 16. Looking ahead, if transaction activity improves and fundraising accelerates, the stock could recover well.

Overall, both BlackRock and Blackstone offer exposure to the growing asset management industry, but their valuations and growth drivers present different opportunities for investors.

BlackRock offers scale, diversification, and strong earnings growth, making it appealing to investors seeking steady long-term growth, although its premium valuation limits the margin for error. Blackstone offers exposure to private markets and AI infrastructure at a considerably lower price, potentially giving investors greater upside if the company recovers. In other words, these giants appeal to different buyers: BlackRock is steadier, Blackstone is riskier. But each looks like a buy.

#2923. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

#2919. How to Invest in Humanoid Robots: 3 Stocks to Watch

Humanoid robots are on the verge of becoming mainstream, and these three stocks are positioned to benefit.

By Marc Guberti – Nov 23, 2026 at 9:31PM EST

Humanoid robots grab people's attention as they walk on sidewalks. Granted, it's a rare sight since this technology is in its early stages, but there is plenty of excitement about the future.

While many start-ups are creating their own humanoid robots, it may be better for investors to invest in the companies selling shovels during a gold rush. Once hints of humanoid robotics leaders become more apparent and finances improve, it may be worth considering smaller companies.

For now, these three tech giants look well-positioned for the humanoid robot boom.

Tesla (TSLA +11.46%) is the most direct, established American company for exposure to humanoid robots. The company has been developing its Optimus robot segment for several years and has sufficient revenue and profits to ensure financial sustainability.

Revenue reached $28 billion in Q3, which was roughly flat year over year. The company's "Services and other revenue" component was the only part of the business to grow, suggesting that Tesla's future growth will have to come from robots.

Net income wasn't as exciting, down 43% year over year, but $787 million in pure profit is still more impressive than humanoid robot start-up companies. While Tesla has been a volatile growth stock, it's actually one of the least-risky ways to gain exposure to humanoid robots. Tesla anticipates delivering orders in late 2027.

Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) isn't specifically a robotics stock, but its artificial intelligence chips are foundational for robotics. As demand for humanoid robots soars, Nvidia chips will gain even more traction. Grand View Research projects a 38.2% CAGR for the humanoid robot market through 2033, indicating the type of momentum Nvidia can ride.

While high demand for humanoid robots is critical to Tesla's long-term investment thesis, Nvidia continues to perform well in current times. Revenue surged 103% year over year in the company's fiscal 2027 third quarter, and its impressive guidance shows it is taking steps to gain market share.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress highlighted that the company's roadmap is on track and that demand is still booming. That's the type of news investors want to hear as 2026 comes to a close, and it further silences concerns about an AI bubble.

Meanwhile, AI stocks have been trending downward for several weeks. Fundamentals are still growing, but the best explanation may be concerns about higher rates and uncertainty with oil, even as the commodity's price continues to trend downward.

In any event, this sharp correction has produced an enticing valuation for Nvidia, making it cheaper than most S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.73%) stocks and putting it deep into value-stock territory.

Micron (MU +19.04%) plays a similar role to Nvidia in humanoid robots. They require vast amounts of memory to interact with the world and learn from their training, and Micron's chips fill in the gap.

Its technology will be part of the humanoid robot bedrock, and, like Nvidia, Micron isn't waiting for these robots to become mainstream before delivering compelling financial results.

Micron anticipates $61.5 billion in fiscal 2027 first-quarter revenue. That's more than a 4x increase from the $13.64 billion Micron generated in the same quarter last year. Micron has established a good reputation for beating the high end of its guidance throughout the AI boom, which makes a 5x growth rate possible.

Multi-year customer deals highlight the sustainability of the AI boom, but even with these bullish catalysts, Micron has been caught in the recent negative sentiment of the AI trade. It has a P/E ratio below 10, which offers an attractive entry point for investors who can wait out the current volatility.
