#2918. Cybersecurity Practices That Can Create A False Sense Of Security

Organizations invest significant time and resources in cybersecurity measures designed to protect their systems, data and operations. However, even practices that seem responsible can create a false sense of security—especially when they’re treated as substitutes for more comprehensive protection and ongoing risk assessment.

For tech leaders, the challenge is recognizing when established security practices are effectively reducing risk and when they may be simply creating the appearance of preparedness. Here, Forbes Technology Council members highlight common cybersecurity practices and beliefs that can give organizations misplaced confidence and explain what to do instead.

“We have 24/7 monitoring” is not the same as, “We will catch an issue at 2 a.m.” This is truly a false sense of security unless your teams have fine-tuned alerts very well over time for your situations and context. That means TP/FP are identified, and actual signals are not lost in the high-volume alert noise. To test, inject a true alert at an inconvenient hour and see if ops is detecting it and acting upon it. Monitoring is mostly a comfort unless you make it a security control. - Pradeep Sandhu, Cywarden, Inc.

The fundamental assumption behind traditional cybersecurity is that all the technology in your security stack will behave exactly as designed, requiring little oversight. This could not be further from the truth. Constant governance and visibility into your security system is no longer an option. It is a necessity that can’t be overlooked or underestimated, and it’s a critical issue that must be addressed, especially as we navigate the uncharted territory of AI. - Kevin Lynch, Optiv

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Prioritizing security by a generic risk model describes the average organization, which does not exist. One bank had 362 vulnerabilities under attack in its network that global data never saw. A score trained on everyone is a statement about no one. - Michael Roytman, Empirical Security

As a CISO, I’ve sat through HiTrust, SOC 2 and PCI audits, and I value them. But a clean report is a snapshot of scoped controls and evidence chosen for an auditor to see, not proof we’d stop a real attacker. The danger is when “we passed” becomes the finish line and the board sees a green light. I treat audits as the floor, then measure what matters: real prevention, detection and remediation speed. - Lane Sullivan, Concentric AI

Many organizations mistake end-to-end encryption for security. Encryption answers one question: Can someone read the message in transit? It says nothing about who is on the other end or whether a record survives. Further, the same encryption that keeps attackers out can end up keeping the firm out, too. Security means governing the conversation at the source, with verified identities, managed access and a record the firm owns and can act on. - Dima Gutzeit, LeapXpert

Treating an approved business application as permanently trusted can create unchecked risk. Vendors now add AI agents and automation to software enterprises already use, giving new capabilities access to existing data, permissions and workflows. Security teams need to reassess what those applications can do as features change, not rely on the risk profile established when they were procured. - Ofer Klein, Reco

Software from an approved vendor, known repository, signed package or internal developer can still contain malicious or unintended behavior. Source and provenance are important, but they do not show what the finished code will actually do. Organizations should verify behavior before execution, not inherit trust from where the code came from. - Ken Ammon, CodeHunter

Early in my career, the problem was, “We don’t know what we have.” Today, most teams have dashboards full of alerts and findings, but visibility doesn’t equal security. If the data from your environment is not contextualized into actionable, cross-domain insights and proactive remediation workflows, you’ve just documented your exposure in more detail rather than successfully mitigating it. - Sivan Tehila, Onyxia Cyber

A common misconception is that if an email passes through a security gateway, it must be safe. While traditional gateways catch known threats, they’re less effective against AI-driven attacks that don’t rely on malicious links or attachments. These newer attacks look and sound legitimate, making them harder to spot. That’s why organizations must pay attention to communication patterns. - Eyal Benishti, IRONSCALES

A green dashboard does not truly mean your business is secure. No alerts may signal gaps in visibility, not an absence of threats. Organizations need security that connects signals across their environment, backed by experts who monitor, investigate and respond 24/7. Regularly test your defenses to confirm teams can detect suspicious activity and act quickly to contain threats before they do harm. - Neal Bradbury, Barracuda

One of the biggest misconceptions about open-source security is that finding vulnerabilities means you’re securing your software. Scanners and AI agents can flag thousands of risks, but without a clear remediation path, they create backlogs instead of protection. For end-of-life open-source software, the stakes are even higher. When official patches stop, vulnerabilities don’t. - Aaron Mitchell, HeroDevs

A dangerous belief is that more security tools automatically mean better security. In reality, too many disconnected tools can create blind spots, duplicate alerts and unclear ownership. A mature security posture is not defined by how much technology has been purchased but by how quickly the organization can detect, understand and contain a real threat. - Dr. Chiranjiv Roy, C5i.ai

Vendor security questionnaires feel thorough, but they capture a one-time self-assessment from direct suppliers and say little about the vendors behind them. Risk changes constantly and often sits several tiers deep, so treat these questionnaires as a starting point, then pair them with continuous monitoring of the extended sub-tier supplier network for proactive supplier risk mitigation. - Yardley Pohl, interos.ai

Poorly executed phishing tests can do far more to damage employee trust than they will ever benefit an organization’s cybersecurity capability. Activities that penalize individuals, don’t result in meaningful and engaged education, or become so frequent that they annoy and create resentment do little to strengthen your cyber defenses. - Kim Bozzella, Protiviti

I think relying too heavily on periodic security audits can create a false sense of confidence. They’re valuable, but technology changes quickly, especially as teams introduce new tools and AI into their workflows. I’ve learned that it’s important to keep reviewing how systems are actually being used, who has access and where new risks may be developing between audits. - Deniz Gezgin, Eightpoint

Mandatory password rotation is often mistaken for effective cybersecurity. Requiring employees to change passwords every 60 to 90 days can encourage predictable variations and credential reuse, potentially increasing security risks. Organizations should prioritize phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, compromised-credential detection and risk-based access controls over routine password expiration. - Gouri Sankar Dash, Tata Consultancy Services

Treating successful backups as proof of recovery can create false confidence. A backup job can finish successfully while a full restoration still fails or takes too long. Test recovery of a complete business workflow in an isolated environment, including its dependencies, and measure the time until people can actually use it. - Shahen Minasyan, Twin Peaks Inc. (TPI)

Access and authentication controls are paramount to any internal system, but with AI agents now working alongside humans, impersonation is becoming a growing threat. These tools often rely on being able to access the same files and systems you can access. It may be productive, but left unattended, it’s risky. Building in systemic limitations to what AI agents can do on your behalf is an important consideration. - Matt Wielbut, Openly

#2913. Anthropic Stock Fell About 20% From Its First Trade in Its First 2 Days. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy It.

The Claude maker's shares got within 5 cents of their IPO price on Friday. My number is lower.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 23, 2026 at 9:47PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Shares of Claude maker Anthropic (ANT -1.43%) had a rough welcome to the public market. The stock's first trade on Thursday, Nov. 19, came at $111.50. It was around 34% over the $83 a share the company set for its initial public offering (IPO) a day earlier.

By the close on Friday, Nov. 20, shares had sunk to $88.91 -- around 20% under the first trade. They even dipped to $83.05 in Friday's session, just 5 cents over the IPO price, on a day the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +6.51%) lost around 5%.

Even after the drop, Anthropic's valuation is about $1.19 trillion. That means investors are paying around 34 times sales, based on the $35 billion or so in revenue the company took in over the 12 months through September.

At what price would the stock be worth buying? I'd put it at $75 a share, around 16% below Friday's close and about 10% under the IPO price. Here's how I get there.

Showing how fast its Claude artificial intelligence (AI) models have caught on with firms, Anthropic's third-quarter revenue climbed 1,127% year over year to around $17.0 billion. The company's revenue for 2025 was around $4.6 billion. However, its sequential growth slowed sharply in the last quarter. Anthropic's revenue climbed around 132% from the previous quarter in the first quarter of 2026 and about 144% in the second quarter, but only about 47% in the third.

Sure, 47% growth in one quarter is still impressive for a company this size. But it's well below the 144% a quarter earlier, and I think the slower pace is the better guide to the year ahead.

Anthropic's third-quarter operating loss was $567 million, versus operating income of $974 million in the second quarter.

The company said the swing was largely due to $5.0 billion of compute bought under short-term commitments, which now costs much more than compute under its multi-year deals. Anthropic also took $2.0 billion of non-cash charges linked to its donation matching program.

Compute is Anthropic's largest operating cost. Its compute and infrastructure expenses fell to 48% of revenue in the second quarter, down from 72% in the first, before rising back to 58% in the third. In other words, the improvement that took the company to an operating profit in Q2 partly reversed a quarter later.

Also, as of and after Sept. 30, Anthropic had committed to around $900.9 billion in spending, almost all of it on compute and infrastructure. Around $70.7 billion of that is due over the following 12 months.

True, Anthropic can afford a lot. Including the offering, it had around $245 billion in cash and short-term investments on a pro forma basis. But a dollar of Anthropic's revenue arguably isn't worth as much as a dollar of revenue at a software-as-a-service business when more than half of it goes straight back out to pay for compute.

Say Anthropic's revenue rises around 16% each quarter on average in the next year, about a third of its third-quarter rate. Revenue for the next four quarters would then total about $100 billion.

That sounds like a fair assumption to me, but it isn't a given. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it expects its revenue growth rate to fall over time. And its customer usage has tended to slip around the holidays.

Given how much of every revenue dollar goes to compute, I'd want to pay no more than about 10 times that forward revenue. At Friday's close, investors were paying about 17.5 times sales based on Anthropic's annualized third-quarter revenue. At 10 times sales, Anthropic's market cap might be around $1 trillion.

Split $1 trillion across the 13.4 billion or so shares outstanding after the offering, and you get around $75 a share. And I wouldn't go above that, because the share count might rise when employee stock awards vest and convertible notes convert.

There's also more stock headed to the market. Up to 315 million shares owned by Anthropic's non-founder directors, officers, employees, and consultants became eligible for sale on the first trading day.

Anthropic is arguably one of the most impressive companies to go public in years. But at Friday's close of around $89 a share, buyers were paying for fast growth to last and for compute costs to drop back down.

At $75 or below, I'd buy shares -- maybe in stages. Above that, I'm happy to wait.

#2908. SpaceX Stock Is Down 39% From Its High. Here's What Has to Happen Before I'd Buy.

SpaceX's business is thriving -- but something needs to happen before it becomes a buy in my book.

By Steven Porrello – Nov 23, 2026 at 10:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

It's a bit of a riddle: A stock loses nearly 40% of its value, yet still looks expensive by traditional metrics. If that rings a bell, you're likely thinking of the predicament facing investors interested in Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.35%), better known as SpaceX.

SpaceX shares have dropped to $136, a roughly 39% decline from an all-time high of about $225. Even after that considerable decline, SpaceX still carries a sizable valuation -- about $1.9 trillion at this writing.

What would it take for me to buy SpaceX stock? Has its recent decline brought it any closer to that point?

SpaceX is a behemoth of a business. Three-headed, fast-growing, and formidable, it operates across three segments: rockets and spacecraft (Space), a global communications network (Starlink), and artificial intelligence (Super Intelligence).

Most people would recognize the first category. Rockets and spacecraft are, in fact, SpaceX's bread and butter, but they're not the business's breadwinner -- at least, not by revenue. That distinction belongs to its AI division, which it calls Super Intelligence. The business generated an impressive $7.6 billion in revenue in the third quarter alone. Connectivity comes second, with $5.2 billion, while rockets and spacecraft contributed about $1.8 billion.

Revenue growth is rarely a thumbs-down, but it's even sweeter when the company keeps more of those extra dollars. Here, too, SpaceX gets a gold star: It reported $4.4 billion in net income for Q3, up substantially from a $1.1 billion loss the previous year. That's a great turnaround for a company investing so heavily in its future -- so why am I not investing in SpaceX today?

Previously, my concern about SpaceX stock was its valuation. That is still my concern; the stock trades at roughly 60 times trailing sales, more than 16 times the S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.73%). Now there's another thing holding me back -- the cost of its growth.

During the first nine months of 2026, SpaceX generated about $13 billion in operating cash flow but spent a staggering $48 billion on capital expenditures, roughly $40 billion of which was on its AI business. That works out to about $35 billion in negative free cash flow for the year -- so far. Management is expecting to spend another $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

Obviously, it isn't a bad thing to spend aggressively to grow a business -- and SpaceX has three of them. What worries me is the risks that come with spending billions on AI infrastructure, where the company faces some pretty deep-pocketed competitors. They include Microsoft (MSFT +1.65%), Amazon (AMZN +3.47%), and Alphabet (GOOGL +6.34%) (GOOG +5.88%), just to name the big ones. True, SpaceX has shown that it can compete in this market, but whether it can create the same strong competitive advantages that have made it dominant in rockets and satellite communications remains to be seen.

With tens of billions being thrown at AI, I want some proof that the investment will pay off. Indeed, at a lower valuation, I might be willing to take that risk, but at 60 times trailing sales -- no thanks. I'm fine letting this one play out for now.

#2904. Nvidia Just Built Agent Security Into Its Chips. What Does That Mean for CrowdStrike?

A brief mention on Nvidia’s earnings call hints at a bigger role for CrowdStrike in securing AI agents.

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 23, 2026 at 10:17PM EST

10 stocks we like better than CrowdStrike ›

With all the buzz surrounding Nvidia's (NVDA +31.48%) earnings report on Nov. 17 and the turmoil brought on by Jensen Huang's resignation and reinstatement, you may have overlooked something interesting unrelated to financial results.

In the company's earnings call with analysts, CFO Colette Kress discussed Nvidia's plans to secure artificial intelligence (AI) agents, and one of the companies she mentioned was cybersecurity specialist CrowdStrike (CRWD -8.92%).

That's a name familiar to Nvidia investors. In September, Huang called CrowdStrike Nvidia’s top cybersecurity partner. The companies were already collaborating on AI-powered security software.

Now that relationship is getting bigger. Nvidia is putting security controls directly into the computing infrastructure that runs AI agents. And CrowdStrike is helping to provide the protection.

AI agents are often much more powerful than the chatbots most people are familiar with, and they're getting more powerful every day. Thanks to agentic AI, agents can perform tasks, access databases, execute software, and interact with other systems.

That's useful if you want your agent to help you create a shopping list, schedule a doctor's appointment, or order a prescription refill.

But there are also obvious security concerns right now, as the U.S. has been hit with a variety of computer-related outages affecting banks, the airline industry, and government services. AI agents can be subverted to do harmful things, such as access confidential records or sensitive company data.

Nvidia wants to prevent that behavior before it causes damage. In October, the company introduced its OpenShell Reference Architecture, which combines software controls with security enforcement running on Nvidia's BlueField-4 data processing units.

OpenShell limits which files and tools an agent can access. Nvidia Sentry, running on BlueField-4, independently monitors agent behavior and enforces security policies at the hardware level. Nvidia says that Sentry can quarantine and stop an agent that attempts to operate outside its permitted boundaries in milliseconds.

Kress emphasized the technology during the recent earnings call and identified CrowdStrike among the companies working with Nvidia on OpenShell. It's part of a relationship between Nvidia and CrowdStrike that is developing rapidly.

In September, CrowdStrike introduced SafeMind, an AI cybersecurity system built using Nvidia's Nemotron models. By using offensive and defensive AI models to identify vulnerabilities and improve protection, SafeMind achieved a 29% higher detection rate and six times faster remediation than the comparison models in its evaluations, CrowdStrike said.

Then in October, CrowdStrike announced it was integrating Falcon Guardian, its AI detection and response product, with Nvidia OpenShell. It also announced plans to integrate with Nvidia Sentry on BlueField-4.

Nvidia's hardware provides another layer of enforcement -- CrowdStrike can supply the intelligence needed to recognize threats, while Nvidia's infrastructure can help enforce restrictions.

Businesses need cybersecurity protection for their employees, devices, cloud applications, and networks. And as they develop and deploy autonomous agents, those agents create additional activity that security teams need to monitor.

For example, an employee might interact with a handful of applications during the workday. An autonomous agent could execute hundreds of tasks, access multiple databases, and communicate with other agents without requiring constant human involvement.

That's a more efficient way to work, but it also creates a potentially enormous amount of activity for security companies to monitor to make sure someone isn't misusing an AI agent, or that the AI agent hasn't gone rogue.

CrowdStrike isn't simply using Nvidia's technology to improve its existing products anymore. It's working to become part of how Nvidia-powered AI agents are secured in the first place -- and, in doing so, to cement the company's position as one of Nvidia's leading security partners.

#2899. NASA Is Handing Out Moon Contracts Again. Intuitive Machines, Firefly, and Redwire All Got Paid. Only 1 Has the Balance Sheet to Keep Winning.

Not all NASA contractors are equally positioned to succeed.

By Jeff Siegel – Nov 23, 2026 at 10:27PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Firefly Aerospace ›

NASA is investing more in its lunar exploration program, and three publicly traded space companies in particular are positioned to benefit: Intuitive Machines (LUNR +11.11%), Firefly Aerospace (FLY +8.20%), and Redwire(RDW +13.63%).

On Nov. 7, NASA announced a new round of awards supporting its planned moon base, including lunar transportation, communications, and power infrastructure. All three companies have secured positions in NASA's expanding lunar program, but their financial situations are quite different. Let's take a closer look.

NASA recently selected eight companies, including Firefly and Intuitive Machines, to compete for contracts under its next commercial lunar payload services program, known as CLPS 2. The program has a maximum value of $10 billion over 10 years. NASA also increased the ceiling of its existing CLPS program from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion.

Redwire was selected to provide power-generation technology for NASA's planned mini-communications and solar tower, which will support operations on the lunar surface. The value of that award wasn't disclosed.

These announcements follow approximately $590 million in lunar delivery contracts announced in June, including $144.2 million for Firefly and $148.3 million for Intuitive Machines. Of course, the $10 billion CLPS 2 figure represents a spending ceiling, not guaranteed revenue for participating companies. Individual contracts will still need to be awarded.

Intuitive Machines has been growing quickly. In Q3 2026, revenue reached $269.3 million, up from $52.4 million a year earlier. The company also generated $66.2 million in operating cash flow and approximately $33.5 million in free cash flow. It also finished September with $463.8 million in cash.

Those are encouraging numbers, especially for a company operating in an industry where developing spacecraft and launching missions can quickly burn through hundreds of millions of dollars. However, Intuitive Machines carries $336.9 million in long-term debt. That's a substantial obligation for a business still expanding its operations and investing in new technology.

Redwire manufactures spacecraft components, solar arrays, and other technologies used in space infrastructure.

In Q3 2026, revenue reached $109 million, an increase of 5.4% from the previous year. Contracted backlog climbed to a record $619.7 million, and the company also reported $488.9 million in cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash against approximately $47 million in debt. That's a considerable improvement in its financial position.

But Redwire remains unprofitable. It reported a $23.2 million net loss in Q3 and an adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) loss of $5.3 million. Indeed, its growing backlog is encouraging, but converting those contracts into profitable operations remains a challenge.

Firefly's latest financial results make a compelling case for why it could be the strongest of these three companies. At the end of September, Firefly held $534.7 million in cash and short-term investments, compared with just $25.1 million in financial debt. That works out to approximately $510 million in net cash.

Firefly is also growing quickly. Third-quarter revenue jumped 259% year over year to $110.7 million, while backlog reached a record $1.7 billion. And unlike many companies competing for NASA contracts, Firefly has already demonstrated its ability to land a spacecraft on the Moon.

In March 2025, its Blue Ghost lander completed the first fully successful commercial lunar landing. Firefly is now preparing additional lunar missions while expanding its launch and national security operations. That gives it an established track record, a substantial backlog, and considerable financial resources to pursue additional contracts.

To be sure, Firefly does have a history of operating losses and negative operating cash flow. Its cash and short-term investments also declined from approximately $893 million at the end of 2025 to $535 million in September 2026.

Developing launch vehicles and spacecraft isn't cheap, and future missions will require substantial investment. And there's also no guarantee Firefly will secure a meaningful portion of NASA's new $10 billion program. Still, Firefly has the largest net cash position among these three companies, a $1.7 billion backlog, and a successful lunar landing already under its belt.

Intuitive Machines and Redwire have legitimate opportunities to benefit from NASA's expanding lunar ambitions. But based on their latest financial results, Firefly looks best positioned to compete for additional contracts without taking on substantial new debt.

That doesn't automatically make it the best stock to buy. Valuation and execution still count. But if I were choosing one of these three companies based on financial strength and its ability to pursue future lunar contracts, Firefly would be my pick.

#2892. A Stock Market Crash Could Be Life-Changing for Investors Who Own These 3 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks

Lemmings is a term often used on Wall Street, and a stock market crash could show why it is important to avoid joining the crowd.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 23, 2026 at 11:15PM EST

Market volatility has ticked higher, with artificial intelligence (AI) stocks getting particularly hard hit of late. For example, Aehr Test Systems (AEHR +21.76%) and MongoDB (MDB +9.37%) are down 60% and 30%, respectively, over the past three months, as of this writing. Cisco Systems (CSCO +6.80%), a tech industry giant, is down about 18%. What's going on? There are two things happening here, and both could leave investors with long-term scars. Here's why these three AI stocks could be life-changing investments, but perhaps not in a good way.

Artificial intelligence as a technology is very likely to change the world. However, that doesn't mean every AI stock will be a long-term winner. You only have to look back at past technological revolutions to see the trend. Companies pile into a new technology, jockeying for a leadership position. Eventually, a small number of industry leaders emerge, and the other companies fall to the wayside.

Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

Along the way, there are usually big swings on Wall Street. Every stock associated with the new technology gets investor attention early on, with many rising to shockingly high valuations. When it is clear that companies can't live up to investors' expectations, the entire group usually falls in unison. If the technology is big enough and Wall Street's enthusiasm great enough, the industry downturn can lead to a broader bear market.

Cisco is actually a poster child for this very dynamic. During the dot-com bubble, the stock rose dramatically. When that bubble burst, its stock fell dramatically. It took around 20 years for Cisco's shares to recover from that decline. If you had owned Cisco at the peak of the dot-com bubble, your entire thought process around investing probably changed. Some investors who got burned during that period may have even decided to stop investing altogether.

As it turned out, the internet did change the world. However, the key story is that the technology didn't make every dot-com stock a good investment. While Cisco survived, many internet stocks did not. And this is where the risk of an AI bubble comes in, since AI is the technology dejur. Cisco is again in play, having leaned into the sector by building data centers. Its stock rallied sharply because of this involvement, but it has also pulled back sharply. And the 18% decline over the last three months is modest compared to the drops in Aehr Test Systems and MongoDB. Aehr Test Systems provides testing equipment for computer chips. MongoDB makes database software. Like Cisco, they are both involved in AI.

However, the bigger issue is that even after the huge price declines, Aehr Test Systems has a price-to-earnings ratio of 890x, while MongoDB's P/E is 400x. Cisco Systems' P/E actually looks fairly attractive at 24x, but that's above its five-year average of 20x, and its price-to-sales and price-to-book ratios are also above their five-year averages, as well. In other words, even after the declines experienced so far, all three of these stocks could still have more room to fall.

It is entirely possible that AI stocks pull back and then head higher again, without the often disastrous industry shakeouts that have happened to new technologies in the past. History suggests that won't be the case, and eventually many investors will lose money by following the crowd, like lemmings, into expensive AI-related technology stocks.

For newer investors who haven't experienced a deep, prolonged bear market, it could be a life-changing event that leads them to abandon investing. Do not underestimate how emotionally devastating it can be to own stocks when an investment bubble bursts; consider diversifying now if you are heavily overweighted in AI stocks. Investing, despite bear markets, is still one of the most powerful wealth-building tools you have if you stick to it for the long term.

#2888. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2886. Innodata vs. IonQ: Is the Artificial Intelligence or Quantum Computing Stock the Better Buy for 2027?

Innodata's revenue grew nearly 48% last year, while IonQ's quantum hardware sales surged even faster, though its losses tell a very different story.

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 24, 2026 at 12:02AM EST

Choosing between a data-focused AI provider and a quantum computing pioneer represents two very different paths for your portfolio. Innodata (INOD +14.54%) and IonQ (IONQ +12.65%) both operate at the cutting edge of innovation.

Innodata focuses on the data engineering required to fuel artificial intelligence, while IonQ builds the actual quantum hardware that could redefine processing power. Comparing these two helps highlight the trade-off between established AI software services and the high-stakes potential of quantum hardware in the tech stocks sector.

Innodata is a global data engineering enterprise that provides human expertise and evaluation frameworks to help businesses build and adopt generative AI solutions. The company serves five of the "Magnificent Seven" tech giants and various AI research labs. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as one specific customer accounted for approximately 58% of total revenue in 2025.

In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $251.7 million, representing growth of 47.6% over the previous year. The company also reported a net income of $32.2 million, resulting in a net margin of 12.8%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio stood at 2.7x, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with its short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, was zero, meaning it had no debt on its balance sheet.

Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was $35.6 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 23.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

IonQ develops and delivers hardware solutions across quantum computing, networking, and sensing. It offers its technology through a quantum-computing-as-a-service model, partnering with major cloud platforms including Amazon (AMZN +3.47%), Microsoft (MSFT +1.65%), and Alphabet (GOOGL +6.34%) (GOOG +5.88%). These partnerships allow researchers and enterprises to access quantum processing power through familiar infrastructure.

In FY 2025, IonQ reported revenue of $130.0 million, which reflects a year-over-year growth rate of 201.9%. Despite this rapid expansion, the company is still in its early stages of financial development. It reported a net loss of $510.4 million for the year, resulting in a negative net margin of 392.6%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was 15.5x, indicating a strong position for meeting short-term obligations. Its debt-to-equity ratio was zero, showing no reliance on traditional debt for its operations. Free cash flow for the period was negative $299.6 million, as the company continues to invest heavily in the development of its quantum technology.

Innodata faces risks from its heavy customer concentration, although it is working to expand its clients. The company also deals with legal and regulatory challenges, including an ongoing securities class action and potential liability from a 2008 Philippine labor judgment. Additionally, it must navigate intense competition from large tech companies and operational risks associated with its facilities in the Philippines, India, and Sri Lanka.

IonQ is an early-stage company with a history of significant operating losses and an unproven business model. It faces operational risks related to achieving scalable quantum capabilities in a nascent technology and the integration of numerous acquisitions. Furthermore, the company depends on government contracts and faces intense global competition from well-capitalized incumbents like Alphabet and Microsoft, which are also developing quantum computers.

Innodata appears significantly more affordable for investors based on its P/S ratio multiple while IonQ does not have a Forward P/E ratio because it is not expected to be profitable any time soon.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Innodata offers immediate, profitable exposure to the commercial artificial intelligence boom, while IonQ represents a higher-risk, long-term bet on pure-play quantum computing. Both are tackling innovative technologies, but between the two, I would invest in Innodata.

For starters, Innodata's share price valuation is far more attractive. Moreover, it's positioning its business for increased resilience in 2027 by targeting physical AI, such as humanoid robots. Training data for robotics models requires custom video and movement information that is hard to come by, so Innodata is using motion capture to help robots learn to move like humans.

Innodata is also a profitable business growing rapidly. In the third quarter of 2026, it delivered 53% year-over-year revenue growth to $95.6 million, and net income of $10.3 million.

Although IonQ's revenue is rising quickly, the company remains deeply unprofitable. Its technology has yet to achieve commercial adoption as its quantum computers have not reached quantum advantage, the stage where a quantum machine is more efficient and cost-effective than a classical computer. It could be years before that happens, while Innodata is already delivering strong results.

By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 24, 2026 at 12:30AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

The best tenant I could ever imagine having is the one that paid on the first of every month without a reminder. Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.35%) has one that pays $1.25 billion a month.

That tenant is Anthropic (ANT -1.43%), which signed cloud services agreements in May to use about 325,000 Nvidia GPUs across SpaceX's Colossus and Colossus II data centers, at $1.25 billion per month through May 2029. A few weeks later, Alphabet's Google signed up for roughly 110,000 GPUs at $920 million a month from October 2026 through June 2029.

That first tenant also just got a lot richer. Anthropic closed its IPO on Nov. 20, with about $91.6 billion of the proceeds going to the company. A tenant with that much cash is exactly the kind a landlord hopes for.

Rockets get the headlines. Rent is quietly becoming one of the most valuable things SpaceX sells.

SpaceX's Colossus clusters train its own Grok models, and in the second quarter of 2026, the company began renting capacity to outside customers. By the third quarter, SI solutions and infrastructure revenue had jumped to $7 billion, and even excluding the newly acquired Cursor, it grew 192% sequentially, "driven primarily by the activation of new cloud services agreements," CFO Bret Johnsen said.

"The industry continues to demand ever more massive amounts of compute," president Gwynne Shotwell told investors, while Johnsen added that "at current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year." A landlord who earns back the cost of the building in under a year is running a very good business.

Elon Musk was blunter, saying, "we could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone," and, after noting SpaceX ended September with 1.7 gigawatts of capacity, "I would be surprised if we brought on less than 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of next year." More buildings, in other words, and a waiting list of tenants.

Here's how I get to $80 billion. The closest public comparison is CoreWeave, a pure-play AI cloud that expects to exit 2026 at an annualized revenue run rate of $20 billion to $21 billion. Its shares have fallen 55% in three months, leaving it with a market cap of about $22 billion, plus about $47 billion of debt against $4 billion of cash.

The two disclosed SpaceX contracts total $2.17 billion a month. That's a conservative enterprise value because it ignores every other cloud customer and uses a multiple from one of the most hated stocks in cloud computing right now.

It also explains why the business gets overlooked. SpaceX's market cap is about $1.74 trillion, and the stock has dropped about 20% in the past month.

The risks are real, and they live in the fine print. SpaceX's cloud contracts can typically be terminated by either party on 90 days' notice, and Musk likes it that way, saying "our approach is to rent at the -- effectively the spot market rate as opposed to sign these long-term deals." That works beautifully while compute is scarce, but rent could reset quickly if the AI spending boom cools.

Concentration matters, too. A single SI customer accounted for 34.5% of SpaceX's total third-quarter revenue. If that customer walked, the rent roll would look very different.

The build-out isn't cheap, either. SpaceX has a commitment with an Apollo-managed entity for GPU finance leases expected to total about $40 billion. That's a lot of money tied to chips that could look dated quickly once newer, faster ones arrive, and a landlord still owes the mortgage even when a tenant leaves.

Still, I keep coming back to that first-of-the-month check. While investors argue over Starship's next flight, SpaceX is already collecting rent, and in a market this nervous about AI, cash coming in every month is worth more than another promise.

#2869. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2867. Nvidia Stock Just Had Its Best Day in Over a Decade. I'd Still Buy It Now.

The AI chip giant's shares climbed around a third in one session. Is it still a bargain?

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 24, 2026 at 12:43AM EST

Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) said on Monday, Nov. 23, that it had brought back Jensen Huang as president and CEO, effective immediately. Shares surged on the news.

As I write, the stock's up about 34% for the day, at roughly $168. That'd be its largest one-day climb in over two decades, based on Yahoo Finance's daily closing prices. It'd also add about $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value in one session.

But the stock sits around 30% below Oct. 6, when it closed at a record $239.24. And I think Nvidia is still cheap for what it's expected to earn, especially with Huang back and sales rising faster than a year ago.

Huang stepped down on Nov. 11, after what Nvidia's board called personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct. Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer, became interim CEO, and the board started looking for a permanent replacement.

Six days later, when Nvidia posted fiscal third-quarter results on Nov. 17, board chair Harvey Jones opened the earnings call by ruling out a return.

"The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said.

The selling kept going. Shares lost around 28% between the Nov. 11 close and Friday, Nov. 20, when the stock dropped 14% in one day. This was Nvidia's seventh straight losing week, its longest weekly losing streak since 2008.

Five days after the call, the board reversed itself. Nvidia said its directors voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after a series of meetings with him. The board also said it got input from senior levels of the U.S. government before deciding.

Sure, not everything is settled. A committee of independent directors is still investigating, and Nvidia said it'll keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

Highlighting how strong demand stayed through all this, Nvidia's revenue surged 103% year over year to $115.8 billion in its fiscal 2027 third quarter, which ended on Oct. 25, 2026. Sales grew 20% from the previous quarter, a pickup from 18% sequential growth in fiscal Q2. What's more, earnings per share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis gained 111% year over year to $2.68, so profits more than kept up with sales.

Management sees around $130 billion in revenue for fiscal Q4, a period with an extra week. Kress also said on the call that Vera Rubin, Nvidia's latest computing platform, pulled in almost $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments. And she lifted Nvidia's outlook for next year, saying the company now expects fiscal 2028 revenue (the year ending in January 2028) to rise around 75%, up from its previous 70% forecast.

In other words, the stock's drop after Huang's resignation was arguably about who would lead Nvidia, not about demand for its chips. With Huang back, much of that worry could fade.

At roughly $168, Nvidia's stock price is about 10 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, based on analysts' average estimate.

In comparison, shares of Advanced Micro Devices, one of Nvidia's top rivals in AI chips, cost about 26 times the company's expected 2027 earnings. Even after Monday's rally, then, investors are paying less than half as much for a dollar of Nvidia's expected profit.

Nvidia is also buying back lots of its own stock. It returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in repurchases and dividends in fiscal Q3. And Kress said it still plans to spend the $227 billion or so left on its buyback authorization by the end of fiscal 2028 -- over 5% of Nvidia's market value at Monday's price.

Yes, a price-to-earnings ratio this low only holds up if the earnings forecast does. Nvidia sees gross margin of 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, down from around 75% in fiscal Q3. And the board's investigation might still find something investors don't like. But at around 10 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, I'd say the stock already prices in a lot of bad news.

In the end, Nvidia gets back the co-founder who ran it for more than three decades, and it gets him back with sales still more than doubling year over year. I'd still buy the stock after Monday's jump, but I'd likely add shares bit by bit over the next few months, given how volatile the stock is. There’s no guarantee it doesn’t go lower again.

#2863. Prediction: 1 "Magnificent Seven" Stock That Will Lag the Market in 2027

Tesla is building some of the most exciting technology on Earth, but I think its stock is set up to trail the market next year.

By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 24, 2026 at 1:00AM EST

I've learned the hard way that a company can do amazing things and still be a frustrating stock to own for a year or two. That's exactly how I feel about Tesla (TSLA +11.46%) heading into 2027.

Tesla is already the laggard of the "Magnificent Seven" this year. Through Nov. 4, its stock was down about 14% in 2026, while the S&P 500 was up about 12%. This week didn't help. Shares were down roughly 6% intraday on Nov. 20, trading around $351.

To be clear, I'm not predicting a collapse. I'm predicting that Tesla will trail the S&P 500 next year. I don't think 2027 will fix what's holding it back, and here's why.

Tesla's core business is stalling. Last quarter, automotive revenue fell 3%, energy revenue fell 16%, and net income dropped 29% as spending on Optimus robots and AI surged. Tesla blamed lower average selling prices and tight battery supply, and it's facing tougher competition from Chinese EV makers like BYD and Xiaomi in Asia and Europe. Third-quarter deliveries slipped about 2% from a year ago, and the loss of the federal EV tax credit still stings.

To be fair, demand for the cars is real. CFO Vaibhav Taneja said Tesla "exited the quarter with our highest backlog in four years, with deliveries constrained primarily by production." Musk said Megapacks, Tesla's big batteries for the grid and data centers, are nearly sold out for 2027, and active Full Self-Driving subscriptions jumped 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million.

The catch is the bill. Taneja warned that rising operating costs "would continue till we commercialize these new products," and that "commodity price increases and interest rate changes continue to add to our cost and create further headwinds." Musk said capital spending "will start to become more meaningful next year and then noticeable like in the tens of billions in '28."

Tesla's bull case is robotaxis and Optimus, and I'll admit the progress is impressive. Unsupervised robotaxi miles grew eightfold last quarter, and Cybercab rides started in Austin in September. Regulators are watching closely, though. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit into how Tesla certified the Cybercab's compliance with federal safety standards.

But the timing matters for 2027. On robotaxis, Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable probably in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year." On Optimus, he said there's "still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks."

Waiting is expensive at this price. Tesla trades at more than 400 times trailing earnings, so its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio leaves almost no margin of safety if a launch slips.

This week showed how fragile AI-heavy stocks are right now. Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia, doubts about AI spending, and the threat of more Federal Reserve rate hikes all hit tech hard. Tesla sells itself as an AI and robotics company, so it wears those same worries.

There's one big thing that could prove me wrong. On Wednesday, Musk said Tesla and SpaceX would "probably" be better together, citing "so many areas of convergence." A merger could excite Musk's fans and send the stock soaring.

But it's far from certain. Musk has said a deal would need "a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders, and that's quite a high hurdle to try to achieve."

Tesla could still be a fine company to own for a decade, with its huge market cap backed by real technology. But for 2027, the gap between what Tesla is earning and what the stock is pricing in looks too wide to close in 12 months. That's why I think it lags.

#2859. Nvidia Has Incredible News for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Investors. Here Is My Top Stock to Buy Before It Is Too Late

The massive cloud backlog that Nvidia noted on its latest earnings call bodes well for this incredibly cheap AI infrastructure stock.

By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:07AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Dell Technologies ›

Artificial intelligence (AI) bellwether Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) released results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 on Nov. 17, and the company's numbers and guidance clearly suggest that the AI build-out will continue at an impressive pace.

Nvidia's revenue increased by 103% year over year to $115.8 billion, driven primarily by a 110% increase in data center revenue to $107.6 billion. Even better, Nvidia increased its fiscal 2028 revenue growth estimate from 70% to 75%. The company noted that demand for its chips is outstripping supply and said the trend could continue due to a huge backlog cloud computing providers are sitting on.

Specifically, Nvidia says that the cloud industry's backlog increased by $500 billion sequentially in the previous quarter to a whopping $2.5 trillion. As a result, Nvidia sees a "significant multiyear opportunity" for itself and its partners. That's why we will take a closer look at the prospects of Dell Technologies (DELL +20.46%), an Nvidia partner that could win big from the $2.5 trillion cloud backlog.

Dell Technologies' infrastructure solutions group (ISG) has been growing at an incredible pace, driven by phenomenal demand for the company's AI-optimized servers. Dell's ISG revenue increased by an impressive 89% year over year in the second quarter of fiscal 2027 to $31.8 billion. Its revenue from AI servers doubled year over year to $16.4 billion. What's more, traditional servers and networking revenue increased 122% from the year-ago period to $10.5 billion.

Dell's servers are used to mount chips produced by Nvidia. In fact, Dell claims that it was the first company to ship Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip systems. So, the company is a direct beneficiary of Nvidia's impressive growth. Also, Dell's server rack solutions are the backbone of AI data centers, helping hyperscalers and AI companies integrate a range of chips and cooling systems to run AI workloads seamlessly.

This puts Dell in a solid position to capitalize on the $2.5 trillion backlog mentioned earlier. Not surprisingly, the AI server market that Dell serves is poised for a big boom next year. Gartner estimates that AI server spending could surge by 81% in 2027 to $957 billion. Importantly, Dell already has a strong enough backlog that should help it capitalize on this massive opportunity.

The company's AI server backlog was $95 billion at the end of fiscal Q2. That should be enough for Dell to sustain its stunning AI revenue growth next year. Dell anticipates a 3x increase in AI server revenue to $74 billion in fiscal 2027. Its backlog already points to a nice improvement next year, though don't be surprised to see Dell's AI server revenue multiplying once again.

That's because Dell management says that its order pipeline is in "multiples of our backlog." As such, I won't be surprised to see Dell's revenue growth outpace analysts' expectations in fiscal 2028 (ending in January 2028). Specifically, analysts expect Dell's revenue to increase by 71% in fiscal 2027 to $194.3 billion, followed by a 20% increase in fiscal 2028 to $232.6 billion.

However, as the chart below shows, Dell's revenue estimate for fiscal 2028 has been rising, and I won't be surprised to see the trend continue.

DELL Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Dell stock can be bought at an incredibly cheap valuation right now. The stock is trading at just 19 times earnings, which is incredibly cheap considering that its earnings per share are predicted to increase by 151% in the current fiscal year. What's more, the stock has a price-to-sales ratio of just 1.5, well below the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite index's price-to-sales ratio of 4.5.

These multiples clearly indicate that Dell is undervalued, and that makes this AI stock a screaming buy. For instance, if Dell's revenue increases to $233 billion in fiscal 2028 and it trades at even 2 times sales, its market cap will reach $466 billion. That's 119% higher than Dell's current market cap, suggesting that investors have the opportunity to buy a potential multibagger at dirt cheap levels.

#2858. Black Friday Comes to Tech Stocks: 3 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Names I’d Buy on Sale

Micron, Nvidia, and Broadcom have all been thrown in the bargain bin ahead of Black Friday.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:34AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›

Black Friday is right around the corner, and the market has been gracious enough to put a slew of tech stocks on sale before the holiday shopping season. With numerous bargains to choose from, these are the three tech stocks I'd be loading up on right now.

The market clearly does not believe in the Micron Technology (MU +19.04%) story, with the stock now trading at a forward P/E of under 3.5. The company has been delivering incredible growth, fueled by higher memory prices.

However, investors are clearly nervous that the memory market is about to peak, and the industry has a history of brutal downturns when this happens. That said, this time does truly look different. While the industry hasn't entirely lost its cyclicality, this cycle is also being fueled by a powerful AI build-out with secular tailwinds.

AI chips need to be packaged with a special form of DRAM (dynamic random access memory) called high bandwidth memory (HBM) that reduces latency and optimizes performance. HBM growth has been in lockstep with AI accelerator demand, but supply is struggling to keep up due to a dearth of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines that are used to make both advanced logic chips and HBM. At the same time, HBM also requires three times the wafer capacity as conventional DRAM.

This dynamic will likely keep DRAM prices higher for much longer than your typical cycle, while Micron and others have locked up a significant share of their capacity in longer-term contracts. With cash piling up on its balance sheet and robust free cash flow, the stock is starting to look like a bargain.

Even after rallying following CEO Jensen Huang's return to the corner office on Monday, Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%)still trades at a forward P/E of just 10 times fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) estimates from analysts. Huang played a huge role in Nvidia's success and his return puts the company in a good position moving forward.

Revenue is projected to grow a robust 75% next year, as the company maintains its leadership position. Importantly, Huang has transformed Nvidia from a simple maker of graphics processing units (GPUs) into a complete end-to-end AI infrastructure player. As such, it is now set to capture a much larger share of AI infrastructure spending per gigawatt of capacity for Vera Rubin customers than in past architecture generations. In addition, Nvidia has locked in a significant portion of future HBM supply and fab capacity, creating a wide supply-chain moat.

While Nvidia will lose some market share to ASICs and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +6.85%), it still has a path to solid future growth and its future looks bright.

Broadcom (AVGO +3.00%) is another semiconductor stock that has fallen into the bargain bin ahead of Black Friday, trading at a forward P/E of just 11 times the fiscal 2028 (ending October) analyst consensus. This comes despite the company having some of the strongest growth prospects in the AI chip space.

Broadcom is the leader in ASIC technology, providing important IP (intellectual property) and services to help customers develop purpose-built, hardwired AI chips. It helped Alphabet (GOOGL +6.34%) (GOOG +5.88%) develop its highly successful Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), which are set to become Broadcom's biggest growth driver as it starts selling these custom chips to external customers. It's also helped OpenAI and Meta Platforms (META +6.55%) develop their own custom chips. Altogether, Broadcom has a clear line of sight to see its overall AI chip revenue quadruple from this past fiscal year to $230 billion in fiscal 2028.

In addition to its custom chip business, Broadcom is also a leader in data center networking, where its Tomahawk and Jericho chipsets hold strong positions in this fast-growing market. Combined, these two businesses should propel strong growth for the company in the coming years.

#2854. The Stock Market Just Entered a Correction. History Says Investors Who Make This 1 Move Right Now Will Win Out.

Stocks are plunging, but history says the right strategy can protect your portfolio.

By Katie Brockman – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

It's been a tumultuous week for stocks. After many months of gains, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.73%), Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +3.01%), and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +6.51%) have all entered correction territory after falling more than 10% from their recent peaks.

It's a tough time to be an investor, and if you're feeling unnerved by all this volatility, you're not alone. The Fear and Greed Index, which measures investor sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, currently sits at just 10 – firmly in the "extreme fear" category. The VIX Volatility Index (^VIX +0.60%) also reached its highest point since March 2025, signaling that investors expect more turbulence.

The promising news is that the market is no stranger to volatility, and history shows that one strategy stands above the rest when it comes to protecting your portfolio.

If history proves just one thing, it's that the best move investors can make is to stay in the market. That may sound counterintuitive as stock prices plunge. However, the market's short-term performance is unpredictable, and patient investors always win out.

The last several years have seen multiple instances of prices sinking only to rebound almost immediately. In March 2020, for example, the S&P 500 experienced its fastest crash in history after losing roughly one-third of its value in a matter of weeks. A few months later, it was reaching record highs.

Similar volatility occurred in April 2025 and March 2026, due to the "Liberation Day" tariffs and the beginning of the Iran war, respectively. In all three of these instances, many investors feared the worst and sold in a panic, only for prices to quickly bounce back.

Typically, the worst move investors can make is to sell after prices have already plunged. For one, that risks locking in losses by selling stocks for less than you paid for them. But also, if stocks immediately rebound, you may be forced to pay higher prices to reinvest in the stocks you just sold.

No two downturns are identical, so it's impossible to say whether the market will rebound just as quickly this time around. Volatility in the tech sector is the primary driver of this recent sell-off, and with persistent concerns about an AI bubble, there's always a chance stocks could continue to fall.

Even if that is the case – which, at this point, is still a big "if" – history still has good news for investors. The average bear market lasts around 340 days, according to analysis from Yardeni Research, and healthy stocks have always managed to come out the other side stronger than ever.

The last two decades have seen particularly brutal recessions, too. The dot-com bubble burst made history as the longest bear market on record, lasting 2.5 years, and the 2008 financial crisis was the most severe economic downturn since the Great Depression.

Yet since January 2000, the S&P 500 has earned total returns of close to 700%. In other words, if you'd invested $10,000 in an S&P 500 ETF or index fund immediately before two of the worst recessions in history, you'd have nearly $77,000 by today.

Since 1929, the S&P 500 has experienced 22 bear markets. That's roughly one bear market every four years, on average. Even if yet another historic downturn is coming, the market has proven time and again that it will bounce back – likely within a year or two.

The investors best positioned to reap the greatest rewards are those who avoid the temptation to sell at the first sign of trouble and instead use this opportunity to load up on quality stocks at discounted prices.
